WHITE School of Linguistics & International Languages, Massey University, Palmerston North, New Zealand Synonyms e-tandem learning; Language partners; Teletandem learning Definition The notion of a mutually supportive partnership is central to tandem learning, where the focus is on learning through authentic communication with a native speaker. Tandem learning involves the pairing of individuals with different mother tongues working together in order to learn each other’s language. Learners can benefit from their partner’s expert knowledge about language and cultural issues, and they are able to improve their communicative competence by conversing with native speakers as well as by receiving feedback. As such, tandem learning is a highly social form of learning which has been used in institutional settings but has also been configured as a form of open learning available to individuals through language learning networks on the Web. Telecollaboration described as “online communication used to bring together language learners in different countries in order to carry out collaborative projects or undertake intercultural exchanges” (O’Dowd and Ritter 2006, p. 623) is closely aligned to tandem learning. While tandem learning requires partners to set their personal agendas for learning and to negotiate discussion topics, the focus of telecollaboration is on discussion, debate, enquiry, and collaboration as part of intercultural project work in class-to-class partnerships. The interconnectedness of language learning and culture learning underpins telecollaboration, and aims to promote students’ linguistic development and intercultural awareness. Most telecollaborative projects involve students with higher proficiency levels. Theoretical Background The earliest forms of tandem learning set up in the 1960s were conducted face-to-face (Stickler and Lewis 2008) in which the primary channel of communication was oral: at this stage tandem learning did not receive much attention as a way of organizing language learning. However, the advent of the Internet meant that students could meet virtually to interact using different configurations of computer-mediated communication: synchronous forms include chat or videoconferencing and asynchronous modalities include email and discussion forums. Since the problem of limited access to authentic opportunities to use the target language has been an enduring challenge in language learning, this too stimulated research into the potential of email tandem language exchanges which allow learners to try out their developing second language with native speakers. Important theoretical developments in tandem learning came with the work of Little and Brammerts (1996) who argued that the pedagogical potential of tandem learning was based on two fundamental Tandem Learning principles, reciprocity and learner autonomy. Reciprocity underpins the collaborative dimension of tandem learning in terms of mutual support, equal contribution, equivalent benefit, and, critically, the degree to which individuals enact and alternate both roles of learner and expert. Moreover, reciprocity lies behind partners’ acknowledgment of each other’s learning needs and styles, while offering encouragement and providing correction. The principle of autonomy underlies the host of decisions learners make throughout the tandem partnership, including the topic of the co-operative exchanges, and the nature, extent, and focus of feedback and correction. Importantly too the balance between conversational activity and peer feedback or correction as decided by the learners is a further aspect of autonomy. The responsibility learners must assume for their own learning and for the nature of the learning is seen as the product of an interdependent, collaborative process (Little 2001). Sociocultural and interactionist frameworks have also been applied to tandem exchanges and telecollaborative language learning. Interactionist perspectives focus on how online interaction can contribute to learners’ grammatical competence, using transcripts of interactions to identify gains in terms of linguistic accuracy or fluency. Sociocultural interpretations have focused on intercultural exploration, the role of the teacher, as well as the influence of socioinstitutional contexts on students’ participation patterns and attitudes toward online correspondence (Ware and O’Dowd 2008). Sociocultural theory has also been used to examine miscommunication and to enquire into the development of intercultural competence online, most recently using Web 2.0 tools such as wikis and blogs as well as social networking and virtual worlds. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions The first decade of research into Internet-mediated tandem learning opened a number of important domains of enquiry common to different configurations of interactive exchanges. Kötter (2002), for example, identified ways in which learners improved their target language skills as a result of participation in MOO-based tandem exchanges: they learned lexical items used in the exchange, including some of their partner’s typical expressions, and, importantly, raised T their metacognitive awareness of the processes which language learning entails. In terms of acting as a resource for their partners, they provided lexical assistance and engaged in negotiation of meaning at critical points. Importantly, Kötter’s research revealed that the tandem learning partnership is an opportunity for learners to develop both their linguistic and metalinguistic skills. Subsequent research in other contexts, however, revealed that learners are not always equipped with a sufficiently strong understanding of the structure of their native languages to provide metalinguistic explanations, raising questions about how best to prepare such students for tandem exchanges. While telecollaboration has long been heralded as having strong intercultural learning potential, and educators have assumed that engaging learners in exchanges with members of the target culture would produce a better understanding of both language and culture, research has tended to challenge these assumptions: breakdowns in communication are common and have been analyzed as relating to factors at the individual, classroom, socioinstitutional, and interaction level (O’Dowd and Ritter 2006). Importantly, Belz has argued that such tensions should not be seen as aspects that can or should be eliminated, but rather as “cultural rich–points that we want our students to explore” (2003, p. 87). Further research is needed into to what extent and in what ways online contact actually contributes to intercultural learning, and how that can be measured or assessed. Further research is also needed that explores the role of task type in promoting the learning of both language and culture online. The articulation between classroom activities and online participation throughout the online exchanges is another area worthy of further enquiry, as well as how this relates to other domains of language learning. Finally, the last two decades of research into tandem learning have revealed that while the ability to communicate and interact across linguistic and cultural boundaries is an important personal and professional asset, such interactions are also inherently complex, at times conflictual and potentially at variance with the expectations of participants. Understanding how individuals work with such complexity and with what may be at times problematic forms of engagement is a challenge of critical importance to tandem learning, telecollaborative projects, and numerous other domains of human interaction. 3263 T 3264 T Target Domain Cross-References ▶ 21st Century Skills ▶ Computer-Based Learning Environments ▶ Computer-Enhanced Learning and Learning Environments ▶ Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning ▶ Language and Learning ▶ Online Collaborative Learning ▶ Online Learning ▶ Second Language Learning goal, or task, can be achieved successfully. Theoretical Background The transfer of learned skills or knowledge from one task to another is a higher cognitive function that is characteristic for humans but has rarely been investigated in other mammals. Examples for such transfer capabilities are generalization of stimuli within and across physical categories or transfer of knowledge from one stimulus discrimination task to another. As the acquirement of the capability to discriminate sensory stimuli in a certain task involves both procedural and perceptual learning, the type of knowledge that Task Difficulty in Auditory Discrimination Learning may be transferred between tasks may also be procedural, perceptual, or both. In this context, the task difficulty may play a critical role in determining what type of knowledge will be transferred between tasks, and if there is any benefit or disadvantage from the previously acquired knowledge for learning the new task, especially in tasks that differ in difficulty of the perceptual discrimination and classification. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Whereas knowledge transfer between tasks in auditory discrimination learning has been investigated in a number of mammalian species including humans (e.g., Ohl et al. 2001; Wetzel et al. 1998), the effect of task difficulty on knowledge transfer in such tasks has so far been investigated only in humans (Delhommeau et al. 2002; Liu et al. 2008; Wright and Zhang 2009) and mice (Kurt and Ehret 2010). In these latter studies, the amount of knowledge transfer between tasks with possible benefits or disadvantages for the learning performance in the second task has been compared between easy-to-hard and hard-to-easy successions of perceptual discrimination of stimuli. It was found that two forms of learning could be distinguished in the auditory discrimination tasks: an initial rapid improvement in auditory learning that is interpreted as rapid procedural learning (learning the response demands of the task), and a following slower improvement that is taken as evidence for perceptual learning (improvement of discriminative perceptual judgments). It was concluded that the perceptual dimension for the discrimination or classification in the easy task is clear from the beginning of the training so that a rapid procedural learning effect becomes obvious in the initial improvement of the performance. This procedural learning effect is masked in the hard task in which the subjects seem initially unable to perceptually identify what has to be discriminated, so that the acquired procedural knowledge does not help to do the task. In the hard discrimination tasks, mice show a slow improvement presumably because of the difficulties in perceptual task identification (difficulties to direct their attention to the stimulus features to be discriminated). Since the slopes of improvement of the discrimination performance in the hard tasks are very similar to the slope of the late improvement in the easy task, a constant average increase in attention to the stimuli to be T discriminated is assumed. Based on this assumption, the average level of attention is the limiting factor for the level of the discrimination performance reached in a training session in the perceptually hard task. In the perceptually easy task, the amount of attention to the stimuli would be a limiting factor for the performance only after the initial performance improvement by procedural knowledge. In the transition from one task to another, there seems to be no perceptual generalization and knowledge transfer across sounds from different perceptual classes and, therefore, no performance benefit in discrimination when switching the sounds between the classes (e.g., sounds with different pitches vs. sounds with different rhythms) in a discrimination task. Thus, there is no beneficial effect when switching from an easy to a hard discrimination task if, at the same time, the perceptual classes of the sounds are changed. In contrast, when switching from a hard to an easy task, subjects benefited in the easy task from knowledge acquired in the previous hard task. Because the stimulus classes in the two tasks were different, human studies suggest that the benefit (hard-to-easy effect) was not based on knowledge of or generalization across stimuli (Liu et al. 2008) but rather on implicitly learned information integration. Integration of information about the stimuli, the procedural context, and the acquired cognitive skills in the experimental setting seems to be the key for understanding the discrimination performance of the subjects. When the task changed, the new stimulus situation was immediately clear and the learned cognitive skill of response demands of the task could rapidly be adapted to the new sounds because of the perceptually easy discrimination of the tones. A possible impediment of learning performance may occur during task transition if the new sounds to be learned share perceptual features like spectral content with the already learned sounds so that unlearning and relearning of cognitive skills is required. If this is not the case, rapid improvement in directing the attention to the new and clearly perceptible stimuli is seen as a beneficial effect in hard-to-easy task transitions. Task Goals ▶ Goal Theory/Goal Setting Task Sequencing and Learning JOSEPHINE COCK, BEAT MEIER Department of Psychology, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland Synonyms Problem solving; Proceduralization; Sequence learning; Skill acquisition; Task-based instruction; Transfer learning Theoretical Background Task sequencing plays a role in all tutoring and teaching systems, whether they involve human or artificial intelligence. Sequencing is based on a component-skills approach to learning. The order in which facts, materials, and tasks are presented may influence what is learned, how it is learned, how fast it is learned, and even whether anything at all is learned. Additionally, it may influence the kind of errors that are made, the amount of practice that is needed, duration of retention, and transfer of knowledge to other domains. Sequencing effects arise when learning is affected by choice of training materials (data sampling), order of presentation, and speed of presentation. Learners and learning systems vary in the degree to which they are influenced by these parameters. There are various approaches for how best to sequence materials and techniques in teaching and training, for example, hierarchical, procedural, topical, and spiral sequencing. The application of a hierarchical sequence for teaching “intellectual skills” was put forward by Gagne (1968). It is based on the observation that skills are made up of subcomponents that are mostly built upon one another, often to the point where some higher level skills cannot be taught before lower level ones. Gagne’s model begins with simple signal learning and stimulus-response learning, which are prerequisites for chaining and verbal associations. Task Sequencing and Learning In turn, these are prerequisites for discrimination learning, which is a prerequisite for concept learning. Concept learning is the basis for rule learning, which is a prerequisite for problem-solving. Although Gagne’s model is comprehensive and moves from simple to complex tasks in a clear-cut fashion, in reality the hierarchy may need to incorporate loops and the possibility of moving more directly to higher levels. Furthermore, although hierarchical learning can encompass both topical and spiral sequencing (described below), it is limited in that instruction is fragmented and perhaps de-motivating for the learner, and it may be difficult to transfer resultant knowledge to other domains. In procedural sequencing, learning proceeds in steps, each allowing for the learner’s “level of entry.” Procedural learning and performance are closely entwined. However, procedural task analysis (creation of a flow chart) reveals that at least some hierarchical learning components must be included in procedural learning. This is because each step comprises a separate concept and each learner has a different degree of expertise for each concept. The two main strengths of a procedural sequence are that it feels logical to the learner and that it does not require much input from the trainer. Its main weakness is that “branching” will create a dilemma for the learner, as will anything that cannot be carried out in a unidirectional, step-by-step fashion. In topical sequencing, a task, or topic, is taught to the appropriate level of understanding before a subsequent stage is attempted, but there is a risk that the task is insufficiently learned or that it is forgotten over time. To avoid this problem, in spiral sequencing, topics or tasks are perfected by means of repetitive cyclical increments. With each return, the topic or task is treated in more depth. The advantage of this approach is that it provides its own review system but the disadvantage is that it causes disruption to general learning through constant switching of schemas and techniques. As neither topical nor spiral sequencing are “pure” in practice, perhaps rather than ask which approach is preferable, one should ask when one should be applied rather than the other, and when a combination of the two might be better. An example for such a combined approach is the Simplifying Conditions Method (cf., Reigeluth 2007). It provides a guideline for developing a “simple-to-complex” task sequence that induces holistic rather than T 3267 fragmented learning. It begins with the simplest version of a task that is broadly representative of the task at its most complex. Progressively more complex versions of the task are encountered and practiced until the desired level of expertise is attained, with the learner being made explicitly aware of relations throughout. Each version of the task can be performed and presented as a “finished” item in its own right. Each captures the essence of what is required but at different stages of representation or completion. In contrast, a hierarchical sequence cannot “run” until the details are filled in at each level. The Simplifying Conditions Method has two parts: epitomizing (the simplest version that is still representative of the whole task) and elaborating (moving through progressively more detailed versions). By helping learners understand tasks holistically from the very beginning, elaboration sequencing can enhance motivation, even when instruction is highly directive. Elaboration sequences can be conceptual as well as procedural. Hence, elaboration sequences can help learners build their own cognitive and creative scaffolding. The main disadvantages are that the task area must be large enough in content (expertise domain) to make the learning worthwhile, and the elaboration sequence must still be used in conjunction with procedural and hierarchical learning. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Effects of task sequencing on learning have been mainly explored in the areas of second language acquisition, instructional design, and machine learning. In the first area, the aim is to subdivide the domain into components, or skills, that can be learned separately (e.g., vocabulary, grammar, and articulation) but also combined in ways that will enable students from different backgrounds and with different levels of preexisting knowledge to acquire the language quickly, efficiently, and enduringly. Robinson (2010) has proposed two hypotheses that are relevant here: the Cognition Hypothesis and the Aptitude/Ability Differentiation Framework. The Cognition Hypothesis proposes that increasing the cognitive demands of tasks will (a) push learners toward greater accuracy and complexity of language production in order to meet the greater functional/communicative demands that are placed on the learner; (b) promote heightened attention to, and memory for, the input, thereby increasing learning of T 3268 T Task Sequencing and Learning the input and incorporating forms of information made salient by the input; (c) facilitate longer-term retention of the input; and (d) lead to automaticity and efficient scheduling of components of complex language-task performance. The Aptitude/Ability Differentiation Framework hypothesis proposes that individual differences will affect learners’ efficiency with regard to allocation of attention, rehearsal of attended information, awareness, and ultimately, extent of longterm retention. Hence, Robinson’s framework aims to match individual learners to particular instructional conditions. In the area of instructional design, the aim is to provide design guidelines that help to identify situations in which order is modifiable and in which an activity can be interrupted without disturbing learning. For example, in a classroom setting, it may be desirable to include short lessons on related subtopics, or additional modules, at certain points in the curriculum. In order to know how to modify sequences and facilitate transfer between areas so that complexity of subsequent learning is reduced, a two-step teaching strategy can be applied. The first step involves compiling a list of all relevant tasks according to the current student model; a task is relevant if it contains appropriate goals and has all the necessary knowledge elements already learned or ready to be learned. The second involves selecting the most appropriate task for each student at any given point from the list of relevant tasks. The pragmatic tutoring strategy is to select the relevant task with the fewest familiar skills if a student is progressing quickly, but to select the relevant task with the fewest unfamiliar skills (i.e., those as yet unlearned) if a student is progressing slowly. As it is known that students tend to tackle easier tasks first and rarely adopt sophisticated strategies of their own accord (such as spiral sequencing, epitomizing, and elaborating), these techniques may need to be taught explicitly. Yet another question is how tools, such as educational software packages and technical equipment, can be developed so that tutoring systems compute optimal orders automatically, while also providing learners with flexibility. In the area of machine learning, the aim is to develop flexible and powerful incremental learning algorithms that have useful and minimally adverse ordering effects. The best orders can be found either by experimentation or by computation. The core question is: how do rules, speed, and space requirements (learning trajectories) influence order effects and vice versa? In the field of computer science, “▶ transfer learning” is used in conjunction with task sequencing. Transfer learning is a specialist term for improving machine learning algorithms by training the system on a sequence of tasks rather than single tasks in isolation (Taylor et al. 2007). Typically, the system or agent learns a certain set of materials or a routine in what is called a “source task” and then applies the knowledge that has been gained to what is called a “target task.” Experience on the simpler “source task” is conveyed to the related but more complex “target task” in order to reduce the amount of time required to learn the latter task. “Transfer learning” provides a way to accelerate training. Learning algorithms that rely on reinforcement are powerful but costly in terms of time, especially when they have to learn “from scratch” and when they are in complex domains. Even so, with “transfer learning,” if the goal is to minimize total training time, or to minimize total data required in order to learn, then the order in which the tasks are presented may still be critical.Optimal ordering of tasks for machine learning algorithms is, therefore, an open problem and at present there is no systematic way to determine how best to construct such a sequence of tasks. A second problem is that of “negative transfer.” Here, learning of one or more “source tasks” before a “target task” may impair the system’s ability to learn due to bias. At present, no general technique exists to prevent negative transfer. A third problem concerns how much time to spend training the system on “source tasks.” Whereas a human instructor can use her experience to guide students as to how long they should spend at each stage, suitable curricula for machine learning have not been established as yet. Although some work has been carried out on “autonomous transfer” in machine learning, “transfer learning” relies mostly on humans for task order selection. An emerging proposition is that workers in the area of machine learning should make task selection a more explicit part of the transfer process, and second, that they should embark on new research to uncover how best to design machine learning curricula. At least three roles are envisaged for human designers in this field, namely, “common sense,” “domain expertise,” and “algorithmic expertise.” It is then a question of using human knowledge to assist machine learning. Studies on task sequencing and learning can also facilitate better understanding of how human and machine learning can be successfully integrated. Task-Irrelevant Learning One model of cognitive architecture, widely used by researchers, is ACT (Adaptive Control of Thought) by Anderson (e.g., Anderson and Lebiere 1998). This model is relevant to task sequencing because it successfully combines declarative knowledge and proceduralization. It incorporates long-term memory in the form of ▶ production rules, against which goals and short-term memory are matched. The most recent version of this model is called ACT-R and involves a mathematical approach to cognition which Anderson refers to as “Rational Analysis”. Among many other applications, ACT-R has been used to model the order and structure of interactions between tutors and students. Theoretical models in this area still have many general as well as specific questions to answer, including: “How can an optimal sequence be determined in the first place? How can it be applied under differing instructional conditions?,” “How can negative transfer be avoided?,” “How can the appropriate amount of time for allocation to source tasks be selected?,” and “How are order choices to be made between subsequent tasks?” As a separate issue, age, prior expertise, and motivation must also be taken into account when models of task sequencing and learning are proposed (Ritter et al. 2007). SEITZ Department of Psychology, University of California – Riverside, Riverside, CA, USA Synonyms Subliminal learning perceptual learning; Task-irrelevant Definition Task-irrelevant perceptual learning is a relatively permanent and consistent change in the perception of a stimulus array after experience with that stimulus array when the stimulus did not directly inform one’s goal-directed behavior. Task-irrelevant perceptual learning is distinguished from other forms of perceptual learning in that it is not dependent on attention being directed toward, nor having awareness of, the stimulus array during the period of learning. Stimulus arrays that are unnoticed, and even subliminally presented, can be learned through task-irrelevant perceptual learning when presented in conjunction with appropriate reinforcing events. Theoretical Background Task-irrelevant perceptual learning is a form of perceptual learning that has been used primarily to study the learning of low-level sensory primitives in adult subjects. Perceptual learning concerns the extent to which the perceptual system is able to adapt to changes in the perceptual environment. While it is clear that during early development there exists a substantial degree of plasticity in the perceptual systems, the adult perceptual system is significantly more stable and robust to change. For example, in an infant prolonged closure of one eye will result in a reorganization of primary visual cortex favoring the open eye. However, in an adult a similar manipulation may result in no noticeable change in the territory of visual cortex responsive to each eye. This reduction of the degree of plasticity in the adult sensory cortices is one that has serious consequences to those suffering conditions impacting the organization or function of the sensory systems. For example, in the case of Amblyopia treatments that are offered during the first few years of life are highly effectual. However, widely accepted treatments for Amblyopia in adults are lacking. However, while there exists broad consensus that the early stages of sensory/ perceptual processing are less plastic in adults than infants, there exists a burgeoning literature demonstrating perceptual learning can occur in adults. A notable example of adult perceptual plasticity is that of a radiologist; a radiologist typically starts their training as an adult and after training is able to discriminate and categorize subtle visual stimuli that have no consistent form to untrained observers. This, and other examples, of perceptual expertise provide strong evidence that the adult perceptual system retains some level of plasticity. There currently exists an active research climate to understand the extent of, and the mechanisms underlying, plasticity in the adult sensory/perceptual systems under the guise of perceptual learning. Recent theories of perceptual learning suggest that attentional and/or reinforcement gating systems serve to allow or to restrict the learning process. For example, it is well established that improvements in perceptual tasks arise out of practice with those tasks. This has led to the view that focused attention to a stimulus array is necessary to produce perceptual learning on that array. However, the recently discovered research paradigm of task-irrelevant perceptual learning demonstrates that focused attention toward a stimulus is not required for that stimulus to be learned (for a review see Seitz and Watanabe 2005, 2009). Task-irrelevant perceptual learning has captured a growing interest in the field of learning science. The basic phenomenon is that stimulus features that are irrelevant to a subject’s task (i.e., convey no useful information to that task) can be learned due to their consistent presentation with behaviorally relevant events. The grounding idea is that stimuli that are important to the organism will produce more learning than those that are not. Task-irrelevant perceptual learning demonstrates a process of learning that is qualitatively different than that suggested by contemporary models of attentional selection in perceptual learning (e.g., Ahissar and Hochstein 2004). In task-irrelevant perceptual learning, selection is thought to arise through temporal coincidences between the stimulus arrays and behaviorally relevant events. Thus goal-directed behavior involving the stimulus arrays and stimulus awareness are not required for task-irrelevant learning, as they are Task-Irrelevant Perceptual Learning in attentional learning. However, task-irrelevant learning is not contrary to all theories of attentional selection. There are many different types of attentional and learning signals that have been identified by psychological and neuroscience research and active research is underway to understand how they each contribute to perceptual learning. Seitz and Watanabe (2005) speculated that neuromodulatory chemicals, such as acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, which have also been implicated as mechanisms modulating attention, are candidate learning signals that may underlie task-irrelevant perceptual learning. The fact that similar brain chemicals are implicated in task-irrelevant perceptual learning and attention suggests that while task-irrelevant perceptual learning may not engage focused attention, it is not entirely dissociated from other forms of attention. Task-irrelevant perceptual learning has emerged as an important mechanism of perceptual learning. This learning can occur without awareness of the learned stimuli and even outside of the context of a task. However, task-irrelevant perceptual learning is not purely passive and requires the release of learning signals that can be triggered by important task events or an external reward (for a review see Seitz and Watanabe 2009). To date, task-irrelevant perceptual learning has been shown to occur most consistently for learning of things that are below the perceptual threshold. This aspect of task-irrelevant perceptual learning may be important for enabling the perceptual systems to improve their processing of subtle, unattended, cues whose incidences are correlated with important behavioral events and as such task-irrelevant perceptual learning may be a general mechanism for the enhancement of stimulus features that are consistently presented at behaviorally relevant times. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions An important characteristic of task-irrelevant perceptual learning is that the learning takes place for stimuli to which the subject is not attending (and is typically unaware of) and that the learning is difficult to explain as an effect of subjects discovering the distinguishing features by which to perform the testing tasks. The phenomenon of task-irrelevant perceptual learning was first identified by Watanabe et al. (2001), when they exposed subjects to a motion stimulus while the T subjects performed a letter identification task. Despite the fact that the motion stimuli were below the threshold of visibility and were irrelevant to the subjects’ tasks, the repetitive exposure improved performance specifically for the direction of the exposed motion when tested in a subsequent suprathreshold test. A subsequent study by Seitz and Watanabe (2003) provided mechanistic insight regarding this learning phenomenon. They found that task-irrelevant perceptual learning occurred as the result of temporal-pairing between the presentation of a subliminal, task-irrelevant, motion stimulus and a task-target. Seitz and Watanabe exposed subjects to four different directions of motion an equal number of times, but a single direction was consistently paired (temporally preceded and then overlapped) with the targets of the letter identification task. Learning was found only for the motiondirection that was paired with the task-targets, not for the other motion-directions. Together these results imply that the learning signal involved in perceptual learning does not require focused attention. The latter result argues against the notion that task-irrelevant perceptual learning results from passive processing of the learned stimulus arrays. A model proposed by Seitz and Watanabe (2005) suggests that task-irrelevant perceptual learning is gated by the confluence between a spatially diffusive task-related signal and a task-irrelevant feature. According to the model, when subjects detect the task-targets the release of chemicals (i.e., a learning signal) is triggered in the brain that results in learning. This learning signal triggers both task-relevant learning for task-targets and also task-irrelevant learning of the stimulus arrays that are presented at the same time as the task-targets. This model resembles theories of reinforcement learning in that learning is thought to be gated by behaviorally relevant events (rewards, punishment, novelty, etc.). At these times learning signals are released to enhance processing of those aspects of the environment (even those for which the observer is not consciously aware) that are predictive of, or covary with, the event. Key evidence for this model has been found in a recent study in which task-irrelevant learning occurred in the absence of any task whatsoever. Seitz et al. (2009) found that subliminally presented stimuli in conjunction with liquid rewards (in subjects who were thirsty) also resulted in perceptual learning. This gives evidence of the role of reinforcement in 3271 T 3272 T Taste Aversion Learning task-irrelevant learning. However future work is required to determine the correlates in the brain of the learning signals implicated in task-irrelevant perceptual learning. An important aspect of research on task-irrelevant perceptual learning has regarded what types of learning can occur through. Task-irrelevant perceptual learning has been found to impact performance on a variety of testing tasks including detection, discrimination, and identification tasks and to occur for a variety of different stimuli including visual motion and orientation, critical flicker fusion, and also for auditory stimuli. Furthermore, benefits resulting from task-irrelevant perceptual learning can last for years. This research has produced psychophysical and electrophysiological evidence indicating that task-irrelevant perceptual learning can involve plasticity in the earliest stages of sensory processing (see Seitz et al. 2009; Seitz and Watanabe 2009). Thus task-irrelevant perceptual learning may be a particularly good paradigm by which to identify low-level effects of perceptual learning because it dissociates what is being learned (i.e., the taskirrelevant stimulus) from the decision processes that correspond to the training task, and thus taskirrelevant perceptual learning cannot easily be explained by learning in the decision processes. Future research is required to better understand the levels of stimulus processing and the types of learning that can arise through task-irrelevant perceptual learning. For example, does task-irrelevant perceptual learning generalize to non-perceptual aspects of learning? Department of Psychology, Kalamazoo College, Kalamazoo, MI, USA Synonyms Conditioned taste aversion; Flavor-aversion learning; Garcia effect Definition Taste-aversion learning occurs when an organism demonstrates a pronounced decrease in consumption of a food or liquid after experiencing that substance prior to an illness episode. Taste-aversion learning is a ubiquitous phenomenon that has been recorded at all levels of the animal kingdom, ranging from insects to mammals, including humans. The adaptive benefits of this form of learning are obvious: a foraging animal that is able to associate the taste of a noxious substance with its aversive consequences is more likely later to avoid consuming a larger, and potentially toxic, portion of that same substance. It is notable that although the term taste-aversion learning is most commonly used in the literature, the synonym of flavor-aversion learning is preferred by some researchers because it captures both the gustatory and olfactory components of a substance that are probably present whenever a food or liquid is consumed. Theoretical Background Taste-aversion learning is a form of classical or Pavlovian conditioning. The neutral taste of the food or liquid is the conditioned stimulus (CS), the illness-inducing event is the unconditioned stimulus (US), the resulting illness is the unconditioned response (UCR), and the subsequent decrease in consumption when the taste is reencountered is the conditioned response (CR). Taste Aversion Learning There appear to be few limitations from either the CS or US on taste-aversion learning. Taste aversions have been reported with a range of tastes (e.g., sweet, sour, bitter, salty, and those that are hedonically preferred or rejected) and odors. Moreover, a range of stimuli has been reported to be effective in producing taste aversions, including those that directly produce gastrointestinal distress (irradiation or an intraperitoneal injection of the salt, lithium chloride), or vestibular disturbances via rotational stimulation. Interestingly, other USs that do not directly produce illness have also been shown effective in producing conditioned taste aversions; these include swimming stress, running stress, and some drugs of abuse that produce pleasurable aftereffects. Empirical analysis of taste-aversion learning arose from two distinct areas of research, rodent/pest control studies developed by the British during World War II and analyses of the effects of radiation conducted by the US military in the 1950s. In the 1960s, taste-aversion learning became a popular paradigm to investigate associative learning because of its ecological validity and a number of unique learning phenomena that were first identified in taste-aversion research. Indeed, throughout the heyday of taste-aversion learning research (1960s–1980s), the primary theoretical questions involved were whether taste-aversion learning represented a qualitatively different or quantitatively different form of learning. This question of whether taste-aversion learning operated under a set of rules different from other forms of classical conditioning like fear conditioning or eyeblink conditioning was theoretically important because it challenged general process approaches to learning. Many early learning theorists from Thorndike to Skinner have proposed general principles of learning that were assumed to be unrestricted by organism or conditioning paradigm. Therefore, in the early 1960s, the prevailing dogma in associative learning theory reflected this General Process Approach, in which an underlying assumption was that the rules that govern the formation of associations should be present in all associative learning, regardless of the exact identity of those stimuli (for a review of the modern status of this debate, see Domjan 2008). The individual who had the most profound influence on the scientific study of taste-aversion learning was John Garcia, who conducted some of the aforementioned radiation T research for the US military. Indeed, in some cases Garcia has been termed the “Father of Taste-Aversion Learning,” and the term “Garcia Effect” has been substituted for “taste-aversion learning.” In addition to developing many of the basic procedural details of taste-aversion learning, Garcia and his colleagues were involved in reporting many of the seminal studies that promoted the unique features of taste-aversion learning, including cue-to-consequence learning, long-delay learning, one-trial learning, and potentiation. It is quite possible that the most influential tasteaversion publication was the set of four experiments in which Garcia and Koelling (1966) introduced cue-toconsequence learning. In these experiments, rats were presented a complex compound of stimuli that included a sweet taste, a clicking relay, and a flash of lights (the “bright-noisy, and tasty water study”). Rats were then exposed to one of two different unconditioned stimuli, either one producing peripheral pain (immediate or delayed foot shock) or one producing illness (radiation or lithium chloride). For testing, rats were presented with a subset of cues from the bright-noisy, tasty water. One test condition involved consumption of water in the presence of the auditory and visual stimuli (bright-noisy water) whereas the other test condition involved consumption of the sweet taste solution (tasty water). The key finding from this work was the demonstration that the strength of learning was dependent on the correspondence of the CS (the cue) to each US (the consequence). Specifically, following conditioning with the shock US, the audiovisual complex produced significantly greater suppression of drinking compared with the aversion produced by the taste. However, the opposite pattern was observed in the groups that received conditioning with the illness-producing US: these rats drank significantly less of the tasty solution than the bright-noisy water solution. In short, selective associations were demonstrated as audiovisual cues were better associated with shock and taste was better associated with illness. The presence of these selective associations was in direct contrast to the prevailing view that learning reflected a general set of processes and that a given US should produce effective learning regardless of its correspondence with a specific CS. Following this seminal work, researchers actively explored and found evidence of selective associations in other forms of associative learning. 3273 T 3274 T Taste Aversion Learning Another feature of taste-aversion learning that appeared to distinguish it from other forms of associative learning was the presence of long-delay learning. The CS–US interval refers to the duration in time from the termination of the CS and the onset of the US. In most associative learning paradigms, the strength of the CR is inversely related to the CS–US interval where increases in the CS–US interval lead to progressively weaker CRs. Indeed, in most classical conditioning preparations, if the CS–US interval exceeds a matter of seconds or minutes, no evidence of learning is obtained. In contrast, Garcia et al. (1966) demonstrated that reliable taste aversions could be demonstrated with CS–US intervals as long as 6–12 h. Because the order of magnitude of this difference was substantial, it spurred new conjecture that the rules that govern taste-aversion learning are different. Subsequent work in this area revealed that one reason taste aversions were able to survive long delays between the CS and US was the absence of interference effects. Specifically, in a fear-conditioning design with a visual CS, following termination of this CS, the organism is likely to view a range of other visual stimuli during the CS–US interval that would be more contingent with the subsequent US. As a result, these interfering stimuli would likely signal the impending US, and decrease learning to the distal, visual CS. In most taste-aversion learning preparations, however, the organism was not given any other taste to consume during the CS–US interval, and thus, there was minimal interference with the target taste. When Revusky (1971) inserted an interfering taste between the target taste and presentation of the US, learning to the target taste was significantly decreased. Therefore, it was concluded that taste-aversion learning does not violate the rules of contiguity that influence other forms of associative learning; instead, its procedures are better able to reduce interference effects. A third, notable feature of taste-aversion learning evident in the work of Garcia et al. (1966) is that robust aversions form after only a single pairing of a taste CS with an illness-inducing US (i.e., one-trial learning). The fact that taste aversions can form after a single trial is consistent with the adaptive value of the phenomenon because it promotes the organism’s rapid identification of poisonous substances within its diet. However, considering the need to identify and avoid predator signals also has high adaptive value, one-trial learning should have been readily identifiable in other preparations such as fear conditioning. Nonetheless, after the presence of one-trial learning in taste-aversion learning was confirmed, one-trial learning was detected in other behavioral preparations (see context fear learning). A final, unique phenomenon that arose from research in taste-aversion learning is taste-mediated potentiation. Typically, when two CSs are conditioned in compound with a US, the CSs will compete for associative strength, and learning to each cue is weakened relative to conditioning each CS alone, a competitive form of learning that Pavlov termed overshadowing. Overshadowing can be most pronounced when a more salient CS is paired with a less salient CS, and the learning to the less salient CS is substantially decreased. In contrast, when a weak odor CS is presented simultaneously with a strong taste CS prior to aversion conditioning, the subsequent odor aversion is significantly stronger than if the odor alone is paired with illness. Thus, the presence of taste-mediated potentiation is another unique finding that originally arose from research in tasteaversion learning that demonstrated a pattern of learning that was different from that seen in other forms of classical conditioning. Evidence of potentiation in the taste-aversion literature was present for 30 years before the first reliable evidence of potentiation was reported in a fear-conditioning preparation (Urcelay and Miller 2009). In a series of four experiments, Urcelay and Miller conducted fear conditioning with a compound stimulus composed of two auditory CSs paired with a shock US. Importantly, they also varied the CS–US interval from 0 s to 20 s. Following compound conditioning with the 0 s CS– US interval, testing the weaker auditory cue revealed overshadowing relative to a single-element control. In contrast, following compound conditioning with the 20 s CS–US interval, potentiation of the fear CR was recorded to the weaker auditory cue compared to its single-element control. Therefore, much like cue-toconsequence learning and one-trial learning, potentiation-like effects have now been identified in a traditional Pavlovian conditioning paradigm. Although subsequent work has shown that these phenomena are not exclusive to tasteaversion learning, the challenges these phenomena provided for existing theories was a major catalyst for much innovative research. the saccharin, but a conditioned place preference to the context. Similarly, recent work has shown that physical exercise, such as running or swimming, may have a similar bivalent effect of producing reliable taste aversions while imbuing hedonic reactions to other cues. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Cross-References As evidenced by the recent book focused on tasteaversion learning by Reilly and Schachtman (2009), many of the outstanding open questions in tasteaversion learning are related. For example, as it has been in other areas of behavioral neuroscience, a central research question involves identifying the neural substrates of a particular learning phenomenon. Once these substrates have been identified, research that incorporates behavioral and physiological manipulations provides opportunities for greater understanding of learning. Currently, there is common agreement that the following structures are necessary for gastrointestinal illness-mediated taste aversions: nucleus of the solitary tract, parabrachial nucleus, thalamus, amygdala, and insular cortex in the temporal lobe. The parabrachial nucleus, in particular, appears to be the first anatomical site of convergence for gustatory information and illness signals from the gut. Of course, other structures like the hippocampus and the orbitofrontal cortex may receive indirect projections of this information. Present work continues to determine if the structures along these pathways have complimentary roles or specific functional roles. Another important research question that is addressed within the Reilly and Schachtman (2009) collection concerns taste aversions produced in the absence of illness. As detailed earlier, although the majority of behavioral and physiological investigations of taste-aversion learning have involved chemical agents or radiation that induce toxicosis, reliable taste aversions have also been demonstrated with a “bivalent” US, like a drug of abuse. Teaching Environment ▶ Climate of Learning Definition Teaching experiments are a sequence of teaching episodes where researchers test hypotheses about how students learn and reason in mathematics. During the course of the teaching episodes new hypotheses can also be generated. These hypotheses are tested through observation and recording of data (Steffe and Thompson 2000). These data provide researchers with greater understanding of how students construct mathematical concepts and operations. These findings then form the bases for the development of subsequent teaching episodes. Professional learning can be defined as teachers working as a community in a sustained and intensive way where they use evidence-based learning strategies to improve the effectiveness of their teaching that leads to raising student achievement. When professional learning is used in conjunction with teaching experiments, researchers and teachers work as co-learners collaborating to understanding what is happening within the classroom (Lesh and Kelly 2000). Theoretical Background It can be argued that teaching experiments developed from the clinical interview of experimental design. The intention of the clinical interview was to understand the students’ current knowledge. However, in the 1970s researchers realized that progress in understanding a student’s mathematical constructions resulted from conducting mathematical conversations with their peers, teachers, and researchers (Steffe and Thompson 2000). Documenting such conversations required working with students and teachers over extended periods of time. Use of the word “teaching” in the Teaching Experiments and Professional Learning term teaching experiment also recognizes the challenge of studying classroom interactions in the messiness of day-to-day teaching experience. By the 1980s mathematics education was entering the postmodern period, which led to changes in the way mathematical knowing was understood. It was during this time that teaching experiments came more fully into prominence as a methodology for investigating mathematical learning and development (Cobb and Steffe 1983). Fundamental to this methodology is the intention that researchers focus on exploring students’ ways and means of operating mathematically and not the researchers own ways and means of doing so. Consequently, this research methodology is not about recording and reporting if a student is right or wrong, rather the significance of the teaching experiment is to understand what the students can do and how they can do it. Over the course of a teaching experiment, interactions with students provide researchers with the opportunity to observe when students’ reorganize their thinking – identified by changes in language and actions. This approach is consistent with Vygotsky’s (1978) work on zones of proximal development. Adaptations to the teaching experiment methodology have developed as research needs have changed. One such change is the use of professional learning for teachers as an associated outcome of teaching experiments. Teachers’ professional learning is documented as occurring in the classroom during teaching experiments and also during discussions that follow (e.g., Cobb 2000). Due to teacher collaboration and contribution to the development of theory, some researchers began to include teachers more formally in their research projects as coresearchers. This departure from the original methodological conception of teaching experiments, by including the teachers as researchers, has led to the evolution of new methodologies such as design experiments and action research. Involvement of teachers in this ways is also the subject of other research into teachers’ professional learning. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Teaching experiments, originally designed to investigate how students learn and reason in mathematics, continues to be widely used today. The important role of teacher professional learning can be addressed in T 3277 conjunction with this methodology. In more recent years, this combination of teaching experiments and professional learning has been used as the stepping stone to other methodologies such as design experiments and action research. As with all research methodologies there are inherent challenges. Being alert to these challenges will assist both researchers and teachers to appreciate the desired outcomes of the other. The challenges that may result from the combination of teaching experiments and professional learning, that warrant ongoing monitoring include allocating sufficient time for researcher/teacher interactions; teacher content knowledge in the field under study, limiting teachers understanding of the experimental process; researcher interest in the experimental process in comparison to teacher interest in the outcome of that process; lack of teacher involvement in the forming and testing of hypotheses, restricting ownership by teachers. Dealing with these challenges leads to many questions for researchers to consider. Researchers using teaching experiments that are combined with teacher professional learning will need to consider ways to successfully work with this combination of methodologies knowing the recognized challenges. This is the short to medium term perspective on learning, focusing on new or improved capabilities built through the content learned by an organization. This learning contributes to the management of core organizational capabilities (Prahalad and Hamel 1990), resource allocation (Andrews 1971), and competitive strategy (Porter 1980). ● On the tactical learning level, we have learning of new tactics about applying the accumulating experience and the learning process: we build new contingency models of decision making by changing the rules for making decisions and/or adding new ones. This is the medium- to long-term perspective on learning, resulting in a process of reinventing and reengineering the corporation (Argyris and Schon 1978; Quinn 1980; Senge 1990). Tactical learning enables firms to approach new organizational opportunities in a more efficient and more effective manner, and to leverage or combine existing core capabilities in novel formations for greater competitive advantage. ● On the strategic learning level, we have development and learning (internalization and institutionalization) of new views of our operating universe or ▶ Weltanschauungen, hence we learn new strategies of learning. Thus, we redefine our fundamentals (our rules and contingencies) for our decision making, or we redefine the fundamentals of our operating universe. This is the very long-term perspective on learning that focuses on reshaping our reinventing and reengineering organizational methods and processes. ● The strategic learning level involves the expansion and reformulation of concepts about the limits and potential of the firm’s strategic environment, where the older framework is seen as simply a “special case” within the new, more inclusive framework (akin to the relationship between “normal” and “revolutionary” science developed by Thomas Kuhn). Strategic learning serves to “leap-frog” to a new competitive realm and “to increase the slope of the learning curve as well as the rate by which the slope per se increases by means of enhanced and innovative organizational routines” (Carayannis 1994, pp. 582–583). The result is what other authors refer to as “changing the rules of the game” (D’Aveni 1994) or creating new “ecologies of business” (Moore 1996). The firm pioneers a new conceptualization of its business, its market, and/or its overall competitive environment, which gives it greater strategic flexibility not only in its own course of actions but also in influencing and leading the firms around it. The effect on firm performance of activities at each level of technological learning initially appears difficult to discern, but is brought into sharp relief by considering the performance effects of the absence of each type of learning: ● Firms which are unable to learn (absence of opera- tional learning) are quickly eliminated from competition as they are unable to develop new capabilities to match changes in their environment and to maintain performance parity with other firms. Studies done in various organizations found that the two main knowledge activities that need to be balanced are the creation of knowledge and the transferring of knowledge across time and space. Many organizations are now concentrating their efforts on how knowledge can be transferred throughout the organization. This is seen to be particularly important in the development domain, where knowledge is a large, critical, and changing component of policymaking processes. Carayannis and Alexander (2002) showed empirically, through longitudinal, time-series-data-based analysis, that there can be too little as well as too much technological learning taking place in firms. This is directly related to their intrinsic absorptive capacity in that learning activities may initially improve performance, but that there is some limit to a firm’s absorptive capacity for learning. Larger increments of technological learning begin to depress performance, until a new critical point is reached and performance again improves. This suggests the presence of an optimal learning absorption bandwidth for each firm, where learning activities should not exceed the absorptive capacity of the firm but also must be sufficient to sustain improved performance. Carayannis (2004) discussed how the ability of an organization to manage intangible assets matures along a continuum from potential to added value where the potential value has two stages – unrealized or realized. When members of an organization are not aware of the knowledge they possess, this is unrealized potential. Through the progression of awareness, the organization collectively comes to understand their intangible assets, but there is no system for putting this knowledge to cohesive use. This marks the stage of unrealized potential, but the value add is still absent. The maturation to added value also has two stages: non-leveraged and captured. Systemic awareness of knowledge may permit the development of superior solutions, but if the deployment of these solutions is constrained by subpar processes, it marks the condition of non-leveraged value add. The final stage of maturity is when the value add is effectively captured and reflected in tangible outcomes – as an extrinsic capability of the organization. We close with the following open-ended research questions: 1. In what instances and through which aspects do learning activities contribute to or detract from firm market performance? 2. What is the scale of the impact of technological learning activities on firm market performance, and how does that impact vary under different firm, industry and market conditions? 3. What is the time lag between learning activities and their impact on firm market performance, and how does that lag vary? Technology in Music Instruction and Learning 4. How does the scope of learning activities affect the resulting impact on firm market performance? 5. How does the level of investment in learning activities affect the impact of those activities on firm market performance? The key issue for this research focused on technological learning is not simply to extrapolate future firm or organizational performance from past performance. Instead, the key issue is to discover the underlying drivers of past performance and examine predictable patterns in learning activities versus performance. WEBSTER Department of Music Studies, Henry and Leigh Bienen School of Music, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL, USA Synonyms CAIM (Computer-aided [assisted] instruction in music); Computer-based music instruction (CBMI); Music technology T 3286 T Technology in Music Instruction and Learning Definition Technology in music instruction and learning refers to the use of hardware and software resources designed to assist in teaching about music and music experience. The term “technology” in this context refers mainly to personal computers, tablet/smartphone devices, and all of the music and nonmusic peripherals needed to perform music tasks with computers/tablets/phones. These peripheral devices include such hardware as electronic music keyboards, digital interfaces, digital recording devices, disc drives, printers, scanners, and a wide array of music software designed to work with this hardware. Online sites designed to assist student learning are also part of the understood meaning of music technology in service to education. Theoretical Background Music teachers at all levels of instruction, including adult community learning as well as more traditional venues in K-12 schools and higher education, are likely to actively consider some kind of technology to support their philosophies of teaching. The modern-day use of technology in music instruction and learning is a complicated confluence of music technology development in its own right, the varieties of music evident in our pluralistic societies, and an emerging pedagogy that favors individual expression, constructionist learning, and creative thinking while respecting the need for conceptual learning. Music, and its development as either a more formal art or as part of a practical cultural experience, has been influenced historically by technology of all sorts. This ranges from the design of instruments and the attendant issues of physics of sound to the most recent ways that music is consumed and distributed across the world. Of most importance in recent times has been the development of digital audio and its representation of music which is, humanly speaking, an analog human experience. Advances in the representation of music digitally has transformed the way musicians improvise, compose, store, perform, distribute, and certainly teach and listen to music. On the hardware side, digital devices such as personal computers, tablets, phones, and personal music players all support music sound files. The development of hard disk storage, laser disc technology, and sampled sound as hardware resources has had a major effect on how music teachers do their jobs. Software advances in the 1980s such as the development of the Music Instrument Digital Interface (MIDI) – a digital set of codes that described sound for hardware devices to use – changed the way hardware and software worked together to serve the needs of music production (e.g., notation, music printing) for teachers a well as all those involved in the musical enterprise. Further developments in music software in recent years have included many commercial titles for the support of music production (digital audio editing, traditional notation and graphics-based composition programs, loop-based composition and arranging, CD/ DVD creation, music video/podcast presentations) and specifically for music teaching and learning (intelligent accompaniment, simulators for composition and improvisation, and titles designed to teach music concepts in a game-like or guided instruction setting). Complicating the background further is the moral imperative felt by many teachers to use the technology more democratically to represent a wider array of sonic landscapes other than the traditional “Western canon.” The cultural use of music technology by wider populations of music makers in many countries of the world present interesting and important challenges for the pedagogy of music technology and its use by all students in schools. It is no longer possible to discuss music technology in instruction and learning without careful consideration of social context. Still further discussion in the literature of music teaching and learning centers on the use of technology as a way to encourage explorative learning in creative music tasks that help the learner understand music less as teacherdominated “do as I do” environment but more as a guided construction of learning. Because the technology can be used as powerful tools for student-generated products, music teachers often see an interesting synthesis of technology tools with the adoption of new models of music learning. Recent development of interactive Internet resources, especially the sharing seen in social networking communities, adds still more flavor to this interesting topic. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Despite the rise in use of technology as noted above, extensive empirical evidence of its long-term effectiveness as a way to learn about music is not present. Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry Much work remains too with important social context issues such as gender bias, effectiveness with students with learning differences, and equal access to technology among poorly funded schools. The question of the effectiveness and wisdom of distance education music learning is still another open question. SLOTTA, HEDIEH NAJAFI Department of Curriculum, Teaching and Learning, Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada Synonyms Inquiry-based learning environments; Science inquiry; Technology-enhanced learning Definitions Scaffolding: Technological or pedagogical supports that enable students to undertake tasks they would be unable to accomplish otherwise. In some cases, such scaffolds would be removed, “faded” away over time, resulting in autonomous performance of the same tasks. In other cases, such fading is not an explicit part of the definition. Inquiry: In science education, inquiry-oriented methods are those that emphasize the active constructing, refining, and applying of students’ understandings of scientific concepts through formal experimentation, informal observations and reflections, designs or other productive processes, critique or comparison of arguments, and collaborative discussions with peers. The specific definitions of inquiry adopted by researchers vary from the formal “scientific inquiry method” (i.e., of hypothesis, experiment, and evaluation) to more open-ended processes of questioning, reflecting, and sensemaking. Theoretical Background For decades, the developers of educational technologies have heralded a great impact of their innovations on teaching and learning in K-12 classrooms. However, to date there has been very little significant change, and the most striking feature of K-12 classrooms today is their similarity to those of previous generations: rows of desks sitting face-forward toward the teacher, who continues to lecture about topics and requires students to perform “problem sets” and prepare for summative exams. Still, educators continue to call for a radical T 3288 T Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry transformation of learning and instruction, and continue to note a possible role for technology in supporting new forms of activity and new patterns of interactions within our classrooms (diSessa 2000; Slotta and Linn 2009; Collins and Halverson 2009). This entry summarizes the major applications of technology within educational research that offer some promise for transforming K-12 classrooms. Considerable research has focused on the domain of science, in part because of the historically high levels of funding available for science education, and in part because science is well suited as a domain of inquiry for educational researchers, given its highly structured and challenging conceptual content, and assessable learning outcomes. An implicit assumption has been that if new technologies and pedagogical approaches can succeed in the domain of science, then they can be reappropriated for purposes of learning within other domains. Thus, our discussion is focused on innovations for science education, letting the reader decide whether there may be possible applications in other domains. The most compelling innovations have been advanced not as general-purpose technologies (e.g., interactive white boards, or the Internet), but rather as specific applications that support new forms of learning, which might otherwise be difficult or impossible. For example, powerful scientific visualizations have been developed where students can assemble their own molecules or create chemical reactions online; in another project, students are assembled into online communities where they can exchange resources and hold virtual debates; in still another effort, students interact with avatars to explore mysterious diseases in an online virtual environment. As research has progressed in exploring new pedagogical models, it has advanced new technology materials and environments in service to those models. Investigators often refer to their technology elements as “scaffolds,” in the sense that they enable students and teachers to conduct activities or engage in interactions that might otherwise be out of reach. Research has typically explored alternatives to lecture-based instruction, primarily because lecture has been established as an ineffective approach for helping students develop a deep conceptual understanding, particularly as compared with models such as tutoring or even peer instruction (Bransford et al. 1999). A common pedagogical approach in science education research is that of “inquiry,” where students are guided to develop a personal understanding of instructional topics through the exploration of personally relevant questions about scientific phenomena. While inquiry is sometimes construed as a formal “scientific cycle” of hypothesis and experimentation, it more often refers to a wider class of activities and interactions where students are engaged in direct manipulation of raw data or rich visualizations, reflection, and conceptual explanations – often in collaboration with peers and teachers (Linn and Eylon 2006). This is a constructivist notion of learning, in the sense that students are challenged to build upon their own existing ideas, and develop a personal understanding of science topics. Many technology-enhanced learning environments have been developed by researchers to support their investigations of different models of inquiry, or specific features of inquiry such as collaboration or the use of scientific visualizations. Below, we summarize these technology environments in several main categories. First, scaffolded inquiry environments, typically delivered via the Internet, support student investigations and collaborations through the use of interactive materials and inquiry tools. Second, immersive environments engage students with their peers or with fictional characters within a virtual world designed to present otherwise unattainable learning opportunities. Third, ubiquitous learning environments empower students through the use of handheld computers in order to provide contextualized learning where students capture observations during field trips or in the course of everyday activities. For each kind of environment, we summarize some prominent examples and offer some comments concerning their efficacy and relevance for K-12 learning. Finally, we close with a brief discussion of the “open questions” relating to the continuing evolution of educational technologies and educational institutions in the twenty-first century. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Scaffolded Inquiry Environments Scaffolded inquiry environments are designed to help orchestrate students’ inquiry, providing supports (or “scaffolds”) in the form of tools, prompts, hints, or structured materials. Approaches to the design of such environments vary. In other technology environments, students are supported as they conduct more open-ended experimentation and investigation of empirical questions, design artifacts, or debate scientific controversies. Across this spectrum, there are good examples of technology-enhanced learning environments that scaffold students in the use of scientific models, simulations, and various knowledge building and reflection techniques (e.g., concept mapping, online discussion, journals, etc.). Below, we describe several environments in order to illustrate the variety of perspectives about inquiry, and the corresponding diversity of technology environment, inquiry tools, and approaches to student collaborations, curriculum, and assessment. One example of scaffolded inquiry for K-12 science is the Web-based Inquiry Science Environment (WISE, see Fig. 1), which guides students and teachers to perform inquiry activities that embody four principles: to make science accessible; to make thinking visible; to support collaborative learning; and to foster lifelong learning (Slotta and Linn 2009). WISE inquiry projects are divided into steps that are completed in sequence by students. Each step consists of a specific activity, including a technological scaffold, such as online discussions, reflection notes, inquiry journals, whiteboards, scientific models, or interactive visualizations. As students progress through the steps, evidence for their understanding of the topic is collected through embedded assessment, which are accessed and evaluated online by the teacher. Students work collaboratively (typically in pairs) within a WISE project, taking turns at the computer keyboard, interacting with peers in online discussions, and even conducting off-line activities, such as classroom debates or laboratory experiments. In one WISE project, students learn about photosynthesis, then download instructions for building a terrarium, which they construct in their classroom, then follow inquiry instructions to conduct an experiment where they grow plants within their terrarium under different lighting conditions. The WISE technology environment serves in scaffolding the experiment, collecting students’ data, and engaging them in discussions and reflections. Another scaffolded inquiry environment is that of BGuILE, the Biology Guided Inquiry Environment. In the Galapagos Finches projects, students interact with scientific data such as rainfall patterns and beak length, similar to that employed by Darwin refining their questions and explanations, and finally explaining the phenomenon under study and sharing their findings with peers (Reiser et al. 2001). A scaffold for student reflections, known as the Explanation Constructor, prompts students to attend to specific components of the inquiry process during planning, conducting, and sharing explanations for their investigations. Collaboration is an important part of inquiry in BGuILE, as it provides opportunities for students to provide evidence to support conflicting or alternative explanations shared by group members. BGuILE attends to discipline-specific knowledge and skills as it scaffolds students within domain-specific methodologies. In contrast with WISE, curriculum materials in BGuILE were developed for research purposes only, and have not been adopted widely by K-12 teachers.
