Cut-and-fold diagrams show surface temperatures created by the GlobeBuilder application A similar inquiry environment is WorldWatcher (Edelson 2006), developed by researchers at Northwestern University as a virtual inquiry environment where middle and high school students engage with visualizations and conduct scientific investigations on climate data. WorldWatcher (Fig. 3) was designed to promote a model of inquiry known as Learning for Use, where learning activities promote the development of useful knowledge that can be recalled in future situations. This form of inquiry occurs in three sequential yet interacting processes: Creating conceptual need, constructing knowledge, and refining knowledge. Students learn within this model as they recognize the limitations of their knowledge in a given situation, integrate new knowledge with their existing ideas, and reorganize connections between their previously held ideas and new ones encountered during the instruction. Another form of scaffolded inquiry environment is that of microworlds or simulation environments, where students manipulate interactive technologies to test their understandings. For example, ThinkerTools (White and Frederiksen 1998) engaged middle school science students in inquiry about Newtonian physics, using interactive computer simulations and analytic tools to create and test experimental models that would have been impossible in the real world. ThinkerTools scaffolded students to more accurately measure phenomena, develop graphs, and determine results from their measurements, avoiding the observational errors that typify traditional K-12 physics laboratory activities. Another simulation environment is that of SimQuest, developed by researchers at the University of Twente, in the Netherlands, where students manipulate variables within a simulated environment, as well as other formal representations such T 3292 T Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry. Fig. 4 SimQuest presents a simulation microworld where students explore relationships between variables by conducting experiments, supported by various representations and inquiry scaffolds as graphs and equations, to explore the relationships among these entities. SimQuest (see Fig. 4) has been employed as a foundation for several research projects and is still actively used within many classrooms and ongoing research projects (de Jong and van Joolingen 1998). The general category of scaffolded inquiry environments has emerged over the past 3 decades as a prominent direction for educational technologies. In part, this is because they offer a well-designed, structured form of learning and instruction, in contrast with the alternative approach of simply adding computers and the Internet into science classrooms and hoping the teacher can determine some effective applications. Inquiry-based instruction is effective because it engages students in constructivist learning activities where they build on their preexisting ideas, and develop conceptual understandings through personally relevant activities. However, such an instruction is difficult to achieve without the aid of technology environments, which support students and teachers alike through their use of structured and sequenced activities, with embedded assessments, relevant resources, contextualized guidance, and welldesigned materials. While more work is required to extend the models and materials described above to the wider community of educators, such efforts are currently underway, and scaffolded inquiry environments have become increasingly accessible to students and teachers worldwide. Immersive Environments Immersive environments, sometimes known as MultiUser Virtual Environments (MUVEs), allow multiple users to collaborate with peers and other virtual characters and objects within a rich media environment in order to address compelling issues or problems. Characters, both real and fictional, are typically represented as avatars, which are digital representations of users that allow them to interact within the virtual world. Two examples of educational MUVEs for science education are Quest Atlantis and River City – both of which have been developed to foster problem solving and scientific inquiry. Quest Atlantis (QA) is a multimedia, multi-user, 3D online environment designed at the University of Indiana to engage K-12 students in collaborative gamebased curricular activities to target science content learning goals, as well as the growth of social responsibility. Students are engaged in “quests” with the aim of solving a problem and improving the state of the virtual world, called Atlantis. When assigned to a quest, students take on a role (as well as the form of an avatar) and use their existing knowledge as well as resources provided to them by the inquiry environment, to interact with other students (who represent different roles), in order to address problems and answer scaffolding questions (Barab et al. 2005). River City creates new ways for students to learn within MUVEs that are enhanced with simulations and models, allowing an interactive, social form of online Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry T 3293 Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry. Fig. 5 River City is a multi-user virtual environment (MUVE) where students collaborate with peers and virtual characters to investigate health and biological science topics within a meaningful inquiry context. The software provides supports for student investigation of data adventure, where the technology environment supports student interactions and captures detailed logs of students’ learning processes (Dieterle and Clarke 2007). Developed at Harvard University, River City curriculum addresses scientific knowledge and twenty-first century skills by engaging middle school students in proposing and testing hypotheses about what the cause of a mysterious illness in a fictitious nineteenth-century city in the USA is (see Fig. 5). The environment scaffolds teams of students to use multimedia clues provided in various locations within River City – including interactions with virtual citizens who provide clues about the sources, symptoms, and spread of the disease. All student actions are tracked by the software environment, which then provides customized guidance to scaffold students’ inquiry. While the work in immersive multi-user virtual environments is still in its relative infancy, the projects above have demonstrated a proof of concept that such technologies can serve to scaffold meaningful student inquiry. With the recent explosion of popular interest in such environments (e.g., World of Warcraft and Second Life), it seems likely that students and teachers will come to expect such virtual environments for purposes of learning. At time of this writing, there is a wealth of research and development activity in this area, with a number of powerful new open-source technologies available for the development of platforms and materials. Still, more research is necessary about the kinds of interactions and inquiry activities that can help students develop deep conceptual understandings and powerful lifelong learning skills within such environments. Handheld Computers and Smart Phones Another means of supporting student inquiry that has been prominent over the past 2 decades is that of handheld computing, most recently enacted through the use of smart phones and tablet computers. Early efforts focused on the use of scientific “probeware” to help students collect physical measurements of environmental variables. Researchers from the University of Michigan offered some of the first examples of such remote data collection devices, where students collected measures of water temperature, acidity, and turbidity in a local creek (Krajcik et al. 1998). These early endeavors were often supported by prototype technologies, referred to as “portable microcomputers,” many of which were developed by Bob Tinker and his colleagues at the Concord Consortium. With the advent of Palm Pilot computers in the late 1990s, educational researchers expanded their development of interactive materials for handheld computers, as well as the technological integration of handheld applications with software running on personal T 3294 T Technology-Enhanced Learning Environments for Science Inquiry computers, or with Web-based applications. Elliot Soloway and his colleagues in the Highly Interactive Computing for Education (HI-CE) group at the University of Michigan developed a small library of highquality applications for Palm computers, including “Cooties” – an application that relied on the Palm handheld computer’s infrared “beaming” capabilities to enable a participatory simulation where students wandered around the classroom infecting their peers with a fictitious disease that could be pre-configured in terms of its level of infectiousness and incubation time. Other projects, such as Biokids, developed at the University of Michigan, employ handheld observation forms that allowed students to record their observations during field trips or outdoor adventures (e.g., observing insects or birds on the playground). At the University of California, Berkeley, Jim Slotta, and Tim Zimmerman expanded the WISE platform to include a role for handheld forms. They added an aquarium visit to a WISE project about evolution in marine habitats, scaffolding students to conduct observations about fish and their habitats with “observation forms” that were loaded onto handheld computers. All student observations were then uploaded into WISE, providing a classroom data set to be used in subsequent activities within the WISE evolution project. New roles for handheld computers are rapidly emerging, such as delivering context-sensitive information to users during the course of their daily activities. Often referred to as “ubiquitous computing” because the user is seen as being “logged on all the time, everywhere,” this functionality can support dramatic new kinds of inquiry learning. For example, students can now use smart phones to create an “augmented reality,” where their observations of the world around them are supplemented with a digital layer of information provided by the handheld computer (i.e., as indexed according to GPS data, or other semantic variables). Other interesting applications of handheld computers are concerned with their capacity to link networks of individuals through text messaging, such as in the recent applications of Twitter and other social networks. These functions have given rise to a wealth of research on new models of student inquiry within social networks. While handheld computers have yet to make a substantive impact on teaching and learning in K-12 or higher education, there is clearly a great opportunity for advances in this area, as nearly all students are coming to possess cellular technologies, and Internet connectivity is nearly ubiquitous. It is expected that handheld, ubiquitous computing will be a major area of educational research in coming decades (Roschelle et al. 2000). Summary This entry has reviewed educational technologies that have made an impact over the past few decades, emphasizing a perspective of inquiry-oriented learning and instruction. It has focused on those educational technologies that scaffold inquiry-oriented models learning and teaching, supporting students and teachers as they adopt previously unfamiliar practices. At the time of this writing, such technologies have not yet gained a permanent foot hold in schools. Moreover, technology itself is a rapidly evolving collection of media and media practices. Laptop computers, the Internet, smartphones, tablet PCs, and many other technologies are still in their relative infancy. It remains an open question how these technologies will continue to unfold, and how students, teachers, and scientists will learn to use them in new ways. Finally, educational institutions continue to evolve, changing the landscape in which our technologies must perform. Currently, the structure of K-12 schooling is not well suited for deep inquiry learning. Science instruction, for example, tends to emphasize the coverage of a great breadth of curriculum topics, which places heavy requirements and expectations on teachers that hinder their adoption of inquiry methods. Thus, the open questions in this area of the learning sciences are concerned with the evolution of schools, and the continued rapid evolution of the technologies themselves. Technology-Enriched Playgrounds ▶ Playful Learning Children’s Learning Environments: Effects on Technology-Rich Learning Environments ▶ Computer-Based Learning Environments T Technotainment ▶ Edutainment and Learning Tele-education ▶ Tele-Learning 3296 T TelElearning TelElearning ▶ Tele-Learning Tele-Learning DON PASSEY Department of Educational Research, Lancaster University, Lancaster, UK Synonyms Distance learning; telElearning; TelElearning; Teleeducation Definition Tele-learning (alternatively written as telElearning or TelElearning) is also referred to as tele-education, and in contexts where technologies are used widely to support learning and teaching, it can be included as an element of distance learning, Elearning, e-learning, technology-based learning, or information and communications technology (ICT)-based learning. The term “Tele-learning” is made up of two component words: tele (from the Greek tZlέ, meaning “far off ” or “at a distance”) and learning. The “tele” component of the term (referring to uses of telecommunications) distinguishes it from distance learning (which could be paper-based only) and other elements in technological learning practices that are not designed for use “at a distance.” Collis (1998) defines Tele-learning as “using telematics for learning-related purposes . . . this definition does not say anything about geographical distance, one way or the other. This is intentional, because with telematics when we make a connection with persons they may be in the next room or the next continent; when we connect to information with telematics tools, we may be accumulating it from the hard drives of our own computers, from our own local servers or from computers on the other side of the world. The point is that with telematics, the distance between myself and the persons with whom I am communicating or between myself and the information with which I am working is not particularly relevant.” In the context of Tele-learning, radios, televisions, mobile devices, audiocassettes, compact disks (CDs), digital video disks (DVDs), mp3 players, email, Internet, virtual learning environments (VLEs), or videoconferencing could all be used to provide sharing or linking through electronic means. In all cases, these electronic links allow individuals to interact, but in some cases (radios, televisions, audiocassettes, CDs, DVDs) the interactions will be asynchronous, while in other cases they will be synchronous. The forms of interaction involved in Tele-learning practices can vary; interactions may occur between learner and resource, learner and teacher, learner and teacher and resource, or learner and learner, for example, as well as between groups of learners, or learners and teacher(s). Similarly, the forms of technological access devices can vary and affect the learning process: mobile devices can capture audio, images, and video at specific sites and be used to share them with others immediately, which is not feasible with desktop equipment. Theoretical Background A number of Tele-learning practices have been in use for many decades; these include radio school broadcasts in Australia, and television broadcasts for Open University (OU) courses in the United Kingdom. They were initially based on a model of “delivery,” rather than “interactivity.” The term “Tele-learning” first appeared in the early 1990s when telecommunication systems were advanced enough to allow adequate sharing of data (initially in textual or data spreadsheet formats, and then increasingly in imagery, video, and graphic formats), and has tended to persist in Canada, the USA, and the Nordic countries. In other countries, the term “Tele-learning” has often become encompassed within a wider term such as Elearning, e-learning, and technology-based or ICT-based learning, which include learning applications through all available forms of electronic communication and support devices (distant and local), and in yet other countries (e.g., India), the use of the term “Tele-learning” has increased as higher levels of broadband communication infrastructures have become available. Individuals engage in Tele-learning practices because of their individual interests and drives (see entries on “▶ Motivation and Learning” and “▶ Motivation to Learn”), influences of formal education (see the entry on “▶ Formal Learning”), social and informal learning influences (see entries on “▶ Informal Tele-Learning Learning” and “▶ Social Construction of Learning”), opportunities through additional online resources (human and other), and influences of accessing or using additional media (see the entry on “▶ Digital Learning”). Engagement due to individual interests and drives (see the entry on “▶ Motivation to Learn”) is a complex area, but can be considered within five major groups – physiological (e.g., access to online resources about personal health), safety (e.g., access to online mentors who can advise about issues of personal safety), social (e.g., being able to ask peers online about problems with specific learning tasks), esteem (e.g., accessing online “drill and practice” activities to gain the highest levels of success possible), and selfactualization (e.g., using online applications to gain feedback and produce work of publishable quality). Tele-learning supports engagement for ranges of learners, and many research studies have identified positive impacts and outcomes on learning also. Ouellette (2001), for example, found that Tele-learning can impact positively on young people who find it hard to learn; the medium allows ease of manipulation (when editing, when gathering information, when trying out alternative versions and formats, as well as when using a working canvas for drafting or simulation of ideas). Opportunities to produce outcomes in different formats (e.g., using imagery, perhaps moving imagery, with diagrams, perhaps linked to audio, and integrated with textual material in electronic presentations) have enhanced the abilities of some learners (often those who find it difficult to work in a textual medium alone) to express ideas and extents of learning. A variety of explanations are offered for the enhancements to learning brought about by Tele-learning practices. Enhanced opportunities for social interaction, using both synchronous and asynchronous means, have allowed wider or deeper levels of discussion, and have in parallel offered opportunities concerned with timeliness (learners being able to ask questions at the time they arise in mind, without fear of interruption, and then gaining feedback that is considered more neutral than it would be in a face-to-face environment). The importance of discussion in formulating ideas and concepts is well recognized (see entry on “▶ Social Interaction Dynamics in Supporting Learning”); some learners have identified the benefits of Tele-learning environments that relate to these T theoretical constructs. Similarly, external discussion leading to social engagement and internal discussion leading to social integration of ideas have been shown to impact learners engaging in “community-based” discussions. How Tele-learning practices lead to “communities of practice” is an area of exploration for a range of research activities. Early findings in this area (Wegerif 1998) indicate that discussions at a social group level are important in terms of learner outcomes when they lead to feelings of “belonging.” Tele-learning practices often involve aspects of social and emotional behaviors, so positive learning outcomes do not always arise from a simple response to a perceived cognitive need. Tele-learning practices have allowed some learners to gain in the short term (through immediacy of information access and online mentor access). Tele-learning can support learners in the wider or longer term as well as in the short term. Forms of Tele-learning (uses of email, chat rooms, and social networking sites) have supported mediators and others in interacting with and supporting people (perhaps in terms of caring for others). These uses often integrate emotional aspects of involvement, as a Tele-learning environment can offer greater anonymity, greater neutrality, and greater participation (e.g., for those who are reticent in the physical presence of others). Beyond the cognitive arena, Tele-learning offers support to some individuals at a metacognitive level of learning (enhancing opportunities for review, providing time and opportunity for self-evaluation, and offering access to alternatives that learners might explore when they are initially unsuccessful). In some cases, Tele-learning offers ways for learners to gain overviews of subjects and topics, offers them ways to see and construct “big pictures,” and provides tutors with ways to support different starting points as well as the size of steps and the distance to learning end-points for different learners. Schachter and Fagnano (1999), from a review of over 700 empirical research studies carried out in the United States of America, stated that when students used a range of educational technologies, positive gains in achievement were shown; importantly, these findings showed that uses could lead to improvements in metacognition (enhanced abilities to identify conceptual abilities) and motivation (increased personal expectations and depth of knowledge aspirations). Schellens and Valcke (2005) similarly 3297 T 3298 T Tele-Learning concluded that: “The results [from 230 freshmen taking a course on educational sciences using asynchronous electronic discussion groups] confirm that interaction in the discussion is very task-oriented, stays task-oriented and reflects high phases in knowledge construction.” In all five categories of individual interests and drives, research studies have shown positive engagement in and impacts of Tele-learning in terms of both the management of learning and the processes of learning (see entries on “▶ Cognitive Learning” and “▶ Metacognition and Learning”). Recent studies have continued to point to the importance of learners being able to combine key features of Tele-learning. Opportunities for distant document sharing and feedback have become increasingly possible by using email attachments or posting documents onto VLEs, while the creation of multimedia materials by individuals has provided for new forms of individual expression (see entries on “▶ Attitudes and Learning Styles” and “▶ Digital Learning”). The increasing range of forms of interaction and modes of expression have enabled wider opportunities for blended learning – where forms of learning can be varied over time to suit the purpose and approaches for teaching and learning (see entry on “▶ Blended Learning”). More fully integrated electronic facilities now allow learners to undertake parallel activities and to collaborate at a distance: for example, to use email discussion and Internet resource access alongside each other; to jointly construct and create documents or diagrams using collaborative software; to participate by observing the discussion of others; or to interact when an individual chooses, without the need to remain “silent” as might be the case in a face-to-face environment. Luckin (2010) offers a model that allows key learning influences in a Tele-learning environment to be considered as a series of actions and interactions within a Zone of Collaboration – coming from a Zone of Available Assistance (the space within which the entire width of resources available to a learner can be appropriately reviewed and selected by that learner), the learner moves through a Zone of Proximal Adjustment (the space within which the learner negotiates their learning with “more able others”) to a Zone of Proximal Development (see the entry on “▶ Zone of Proximal Development”) (the space within which the learner identifies goals and undertakes activities to complete one or more tasks). It is clear that this model highlights the key importance of the learner both developing and using metacognitive processes when undertaking learning actions and interactions. However, it should also be noted that certain negative aspects continue to be identified with Tele-learning practices. Of particular recent importance has been the ease with which learners can simply “copy and paste,” which fails to lead to understanding or a transfer of knowledge or ideas because the processes of engagement with and manipulation of information and ideas are lacking. In such cases, it is particularly important for tutors and teachers to give guidance and advice to learners as well as consider how to instigate, develop, and ensure learner independence of action. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Although studies have shown that different aspects of learning can be impacted by Tele-learning practices, questions still remain as to the extents of these impacts and whether such measures are themselves valuable, or whether impacts for learners are related far more to individual, personal, or affective characteristics that need to be explored concurrently. Concerns raised about a potential reduction of cognitive interactions for the learner when Tele-learning practices are used (e.g., due to decreased levels of handwriting) have often been balanced with a recognition of positive impacts arising (learners finding that typing allows an easier match of cognitive activity to levels of attention, engagement, or motor interactions). Although some motivational aspects of Tele-learning involvement have been studied (both motivations that engage the learner, as well as motivations arising after use by the learner), many questions remain at this time about how Tele-learning interacts with and impacts on motivational aspects such as self-efficacy, learning goals, and self-confidence. Knowing more about how Tele-learning practices can be developed effectively when teachers or mentors are involved has been highlighted as an important research need by some authors. For example, Laferrière and Breuleux (2002) state that: “the complexity of the educational transformations that the teaching profession is facing calls for powerful conceptual tools to Tele-Learning think about learning and leading. We are collectively faced with new questions that cannot be answered from our past experiences. For example, what does it mean to ‘lead’ a community of learners, considering that such communities cannot simply be engineered but that they are highly complex, self-organizing, and ecological entities?” In this context, Wasson and Mørch (2000) highlight four different collaboration patterns arising from their research (adaptation, coordinated desynchronization, informal language, and constructive commenting), and argue that “what these examples illustrate is that training and practice in the art of collaboration is equally, if not more important, than just being trained in using the tools.” More recent research from Salmon (2004) has continued to identify the key roles of e-moderation in supporting teaching and learning online, while Ertl, Reiserer, and Mandl (2005) explore how content schemes and collaboration scripts can impact outcomes for students; their work also highlights the importance of relating effective supportive practices and identification of outcomes through research to specific technologies, as well as to specific concepts of learning. Oubenaissa-Giardina (2007) highlights the need to consider “the nonavailability of design tools that consider learners’ perspectives, beliefs, and how those elements affect the learners’ socio-cognitive and metacognitive interaction. Therefore, it is clear that we need to understand how interactions are affected by personal and cultural differences.” The complexity of this field is further deepened by the need to consider practices and related outcomes in specific subject domains (e.g., uses and outcomes in medicine as described by Moser et al. 2003) and the development and use of specific learning resources (see Busetti et al. 2007). Tele-learning practices are undoubtedly supporting the management and processes of learning for a range of individuals. Although research has identified uses and impacts, outcomes relating to particular groups of learners (e.g., those who are working at the level of physiological needs, safety needs, those who are shy, those who find it hard to learn, and those who are emotionally unstable) have not always been specifically focused on and delineated. Indeed, some studies have simply grouped outcomes arising from potentially disparate groups together, appearing also to assume similarities of learning approach across all of those T 3299 individuals. As Tele-learning practices move from more focused uses in higher education contexts to uses in school and informal learning contexts increasingly, research studies will need to be more specifically targeted if they are to answer fundamental questions and allow findings to be applied usefully to specific groups of users in terms of practice and policy. Technologically, questions also remain. Even in countries where broadband-linked technologies are now well established, full interoperability and ease of resource access are still not always easy. Learners can find that their applications (e.g., videoconferencing or VLEs) do not interoperate with those used by other learners or mentors and some systems do not allow ease of sharing documents. While some nations have attempted to address these issues through national standards and national system provision, the issue of ease of access and interoperability across nations is yet to be addressed. Over the past 20 years, research has explored learning impacts arising as successive Tele-learning technologies have been developed and implemented. New technologies will continue to be developed and applied to educational contexts, and there is clearly a continued need for research in this area. The development of Telelearning practices within an increasing range of nations is an important topic in itself. Although questions are sometimes raised about the priorities of such research, Panda and Chaudhary (2001) say in the context of Telelearning developments in India: “the fact is that India needs the jet and the bullock cart, the global connections and the local delivery. CHURCH Department of Psychology, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA Synonyms Duration discrimination; Timing Definition Temporal learning refers to the acquisition of knowledge about the physical time between events. The events may be stimuli or responses. Thus, a person with experience at a particular traffic light may learn the duration of the red light, the interval between the yellow and red light, the time from the change in one of the lights until a response can be made on the accelerator or brake pedal, the temporal relationship between the responses on the two pedals, etc. This knowledge is usually described in terms of psychological time between events, which is referred to as temporal perception, or equivalently, the subjective representation of physical time. Temporal learning involves more than just the perception of time; it also involves temporal memory (the remembered psychological time) and temporal decision that is based on a comparison between temporal perception and temporal memory. Theoretical Background Humans and other animals live in a physical world characterized by space and time. With experience they learn the distinctive features of many locations, the relationship of these locations to each other, their own present location, and how to navigate to other locations. This is referred to as spatial learning, and it is done in a three-dimensional world. With experience they also learn the times at which events happen, and their durations. This is referred to as temporal learning, and it requires only a single dimension. In thinking about temporal learning, it is important to distinguish between physical time and psychological time. Physical time refers to time as measured by physical instruments (e.g., clocks); psychological time refers to time as measured by biological instruments (e.g., behavior). To distinguish psychological time from T physical time, it is useful to consider an example: A person is presented tones with durations randomly selected from a list of 11 durations (e.g., 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, and 2.0 s) and asked to report the apparent durations of the tones. The physical duration is the number of seconds recorded by an accurate clock; the psychological duration is the reported duration. There are many different ways that a person might be asked to report a duration. Some of the possibilities are as follows: (a) report the number of “seconds”; (b) report the duration on a scale of 1–7, or (c) report whether the tone was “short” or “long.” These reports may be spoken or written, or they may be based on pressing a key on a computer keyboard. Another way that a person might be asked to report a duration is to hold down a key to reproduce the duration. The different methods to obtain a report of the psychological duration produce similar results. One of the advantages of the methods that do not require spoken or written language is that they may be used for nonhuman, as well as human, animals. This permits comparison of the psychological timing of different species. The relationship between the psychological duration and the physical duration is known as the psychophysical function, that is, the function relating the duration reported by a person to the duration measured with a physical device. Although it seems natural to time the duration of a continuous stimulus, what does it mean to time the duration between two brief stimuli, for example, the duration between two clicks? Between the two clicks there is only “empty time,” and how is it possible to time the duration of nothing? Humans and other animals can easily time the duration between two clicks, and philosophers and psychologists have spent considerable time and effort to explain how this can be done. The current standard approach of psychologists is to introduce the concept of a “time marker” that is a physical stimulus, and a psychological process that changes in a regular way with physical time since the onset of the time marker. This psychological process is usually called an “internal clock,” but some writers prefer to use other names. To explain how it is possible to time the duration of nothing, the approach is to say that a click (an external stimulus) is a time marker, and an internal clock times begins at the time marker and can be read at any time, such as the next click. 3301 T 3302 T Temporal Learning in Humans and Other Animals Four types of time markers have been identified: (a) external stimuli, (b) contexts, (c) outcomes, and (d) responses. The time marker may be the onset or termination of an external stimulus (such as a tone or a click). It may also be a context, which refers to a relatively unchanging environmental location. Thus a rat can learn to expect food two minutes after it has been put in a particular box. Time markers also may be outcomes, such as rewards or punishments. This makes it possible for a person or a rat to respond differentially to different sequences of reward (R) and nonreward (N), such as (RNRNRN. . . or RRNRRN. . .). Thus, they can anticipate the time of the next food on the basis of the time of delivery of the last food. Time markers may also be responses. For example, a person or a rat can learn to respond slowly if a long interval between responses is necessary in order to obtain food. They can also learn to time from multiple time markers (simultaneous temporal processing). In his famous textbook, William James (1890) provided a thoughtful review of the perception and learning of time in humans. In his lectures, Ivan Pavlov (1927) provided strong evidence of the perception and learning of time by dogs. These approaches to the study of human and nonhuman animal time perception and learning were quite different. The similarities are now more clearly understood (1993). Two types of explanations of temporal learning have been extensively used – explanation with principles, and explanation by processes. The principles are “if-then” statements, such as “if food is delivered to a rat at a fixed time after the onset of a stimulus, then the rat will learn to anticipate the food after the onset of the stimulus.” A deduction from this principles follows from a procedural statement that “food was delivered to a rat at a fixed time,” and a definition of a behavioral measure of “anticipation.” Some of the most general principles have been referred to as “laws.” The principles of scalar timing have been intensively investigated (Gibbon 1991). They are impressive because of their ability to provide quantitative predictions of behavior of individuals and to apply to a wide range of species. These principles provide a way to make predictions about behavior from a single physical time to all other physical times. The scalar timing principles are as follows: (a) The mean psychological time of an outcome is a linear function of the mean physical time; (b) The standard deviation of the psychological time of an outcome is proportional to the mean physical time; (c) The ratio of the standard deviation of the psychological time to the mean of the psychological time is a constant; and (d) The distribution of relative psychological times of an outcome is the same for all intervals. These principles provide an excellent approximation to observed behavior under most conditions. A deeper understanding of the conditions under which there are systematic deviations from the scalar property have revealed important clues about the underlying neural basis for timing. Standard learning theories are focused on the determinants of strength of associations, and do not make predictions about temporal learning. Other theories have been developed to account for temporal learning but do not make predictions about associative learning. Three approaches have been used for the integration of these two types of theories: (a) modification of a theory of associative strength to include predictions regarding temporal learning, (b) modifications of a theory of temporal learning to include predictions regarding associative learning, and (c) development of a hybrid model to do both. Some theories make quantitative predictions of times of individual responses of individual participants. Ideally, these models will be simple, and easy to modify and test. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions A major open question for scientific research on temporal learning in the twenty-first century concerns the explanation of temporal learning. In the twentieth century most effort on temporal learning was put into the discovery of facts, and the organization of these facts into general principles. The enormous developments in neuroscience, some of which has been devoted to temporal learning, is now likely to lead to discoveries regarding the biological basis of internal clocks, temporal perception, memory, and decision processes. There have also been enormous developments in computational sciences, some of which have been devoted to temporal learning. This is likely to establish mathematical theories of the relationship between temporal experience and timed behavior. A thorough knowledge of the temporal experiences of an individual may be sufficient to lead to accurate predictions of behavior. It is also possible that observation of the temporal behavior may lead to an accurate diagnosis of the experiences of an individual. MCDANIEL Department of Psychology, Washington University, Saint Louis, MO, USA Synonyms Retrieval practice; Testing effect Definition In educational settings, tests are generally viewed as a high-stakes means of assessing learning. Much research, however, suggests that tests can be used to promote learning, rather than merely evaluate it. In fact, research has shown that taking a test on studied material improves retention of the material beyond merely restudying the material. This phenomenon is termed the testing effect and has been demonstrated to enhance learning even with retention intervals of months (see McDaniel et al. 2011). While the concept that testing improves memory has existed for hundreds of years, it has not received wide attention in the educational community. Only recently have researchers begun to explore both the applied potential and the theoretical nuances of test-enhanced learning. Theoretical Background In 1620, Bacon argued that: “if you read a piece of text through twenty times, you will not learn it by heart so easily as if you read it ten times while attempting to recite from time to time and consulting the text when your memory fails” (F. Bacon, 1620/2000 cited in Roediger and Karpicke 2006, p. 181). The earliest experiments to assess this theory took place in the early 1900s and the results suggested that, in comparison to restudying material, a certain period of studying followed by self-testing in the form of recitation led to superior performance on subsequent tests (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). Two theories attempt to explain the direct benefits of the testing effect. The ▶ transfer-appropriate processing theory suggests that initial tests improve performance on final tests because they stimulate learners to use the same retrieval processes that are required on the final tests. This theory cannot accommodate all findings, however. For instance, matched formats on initial and final tests (e.g., recognition vs recall) do not always produce higher final test scores than mismatched formats (see Rohrer et al. 2010). Another theory suggests that the ▶ effortful retrieval demanded by tests is responsible for the testing effect. Effortful retrieval may stimulate further strengthening or variability of encoding of the target content, more so than additional study (see Roediger et al. in press). Support for this theory stems from the common finding that recall quizzes (i.e., short answer, cued recall, free recall) produce a greater testing effect than recognition tests (i.e., multiple-choice), even when the final test is a recognition test (Rohrer et al. 2010). In addition, there are many indirect reasons why testing might enhance learning. For example, frequent quizzing may reduce anxiety on summative exams and thus improve performance. Furthermore, quizzing generally involves feedback, which increases exposure and review opportunities. Quizzes also serve a metacognitive function: students are more attuned to what they know and what they do not know, which can help them target their studying. These benefits are especially pertinent to authentic classroom settings and provide further justification to incorporate low-stakes quizzing in schools. Important Scientific Research and Open Questions Test-Enhanced Learning in the Laboratory When studying the testing effect in the laboratory, the experimenter generally presents materials for participants to study (often a word list or a list of pairedassociates). One group of participants is then given one or more initial tests prior to the final test. Final test performance is then compared to control conditions. In one type of control, participants only study the material once. In a more rigorous control, participants have the opportunity to study the material the same Test-Enhanced Learning number of times that the experimental group is tested. Generally, the results show the testing group outperforming both the single study and restudy conditions (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). Furthermore, research indicates that the testing effect is augmented as the delay increases between the initial test (or study) and final testing. Several study sessions tend to result in high performance on a test administered immediately after studying. This may explain why many students choose to “cram” immediately before an important test. It is virtually undisputed, however, that cramming does not lead to long-term retention of studied material. When retention is measured after a delay, participants who took multiple initial tests perform better than participants who engaged in the same number of study sessions. This effect becomes more pronounced as the number of initial tests increases (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). An issue that follows from the above finding concerns the optimal spacing of multiple initial tests. With an expanding schedule, the interval between successive initial tests gradually increases. For example, if 3 min elapse between the first and second initial tests, 5 min would elapse between the second and third initial tests, and so on. In contrast, an equally spaced schedule results when the same amount of time elapses between each initial test. Some researchers argue that an expanding schedule is optimal because the spacing gradually increases the difficulty of retrieval, thus promoting later retention. Findings have not consistently supported this theory, however. While some research suggests that an expanding schedule is preferable, other studies indicate that an equal schedule is more beneficial; many find no difference in final performance after an expanding schedule relative to an equal schedule. Regardless, both spaced schedules have consistently been shown to result in superior final test performance than massed quizzing (Roediger and Karpicke 2006). Researchers have also examined the most beneficial format of the initial tests. Many studies have found that short answer initial tests result in superior final test performance in comparison to multiple-choice initial tests. These findings support the effortful retrieval theory, as multiple-choice questions require significantly less effortful retrieval than short answer questions. Furthermore, learners tend to perform better on final T 3305 tests when initial tests require more effortful retrieval, regardless of initial test format. Researchers measured learners’ response times on initial test questions and found that learners exhibited superior retention for items that took them longer to respond to, in comparison to questions that were answered quickly on the initial tests (thereby indicating that the item demanded little effortful retrieval; see Rohrer et al. 2010, for review). Published 1991 Description In this important theoretical treatist, Jean Lave, anthropologist, and Etienne Wenger, computer scientist, push forward the notion of situated learning - that learning is fundamentally a social process. The authors maintain that learning viewed as situated activity has as its central defining characteristic a process they call legitimate peripheral participation (LPP). id:W14494740.title: Web Usage Mining for a Better Web-Based Learning Environment
id:W14494740.text: Web Usage Mining for a Better Web-Based Learning Environment Osmar R. Zaïane Department of Computing Science, University of Alberta Edmonton, Alberta, Canada zaiane@cs.ualberta.ca Abstract Web-based technology is often the technology of choice for distance education given the ease of use of the tools to browse the resources on the Web, the relative affordability of accessing the ubiquitous Web, and the simplicity of deploying and maintaining resources on the WorldWide Web. Many sophisticated web-based learning environments have been developed and are in use around the world. The same technology is being used for electronic commerce and has become extremely popular. However, while there are clever tools developed to understand on-line customer’s behaviours in order to increase sales and profit, there is very little done to automatically discover access patterns to understand learners’ behaviour on web-based distance learning. Educators, using on-line learning environments and tools, have very little support to evaluate learners’ activities and discriminate between different learners’ on-line behaviours. In this paper, we discuss some data mining and machine learning techniques that could be used to enhance web-based learning environments for the educator to better evaluate the leaning process, as well as for the learners to help them in their learning endeavour. 1. Introduction and background With the rapid development of the World-Wide Web (WWW), the increased popularity and ease of use of its tools, the World-Wide Web is becoming the most important media for collecting, sharing and distributing information. Many organizations and corporations provide information and services on the Web such as automated customer support, on-line shopping, and a myriad of resources and applications. Web-based applications and environments for electronic commerce, distance education, on-line collaboration, news broadcasts, etc., are becoming common practice and widespread. The WWW is becoming ubiquitous and an ordinary tool for everyday activities of common people, from a child sharing music files with friends to a senior receiving photographs and messages from grandchildren across the world. It is typical to see web pages for courses in all fields taught at universities and colleges providing course notes and related resources even if these courses are delivered in traditional classrooms. It is not surprising that the Web is the means of choice to architect modern advanced distance education systems. Distance education is a field where web-based technology was very quickly adopted and used for course delivery and knowledge sharing. Typical web-based learning environments such as Virtual-U [5] and Web-CT [13] include course content delivery tools, synchronous and asynchronous conferencing systems, polling and quiz modules, virtual workspaces for sharing resources, white boards, grade reporting systems, logbooks, assignment submission components, etc. In a virtual classroom, educators provide resources such as text, multimedia and simulations, and moderate and animate discussions. Remote learners are encouraged to peruse the resources and participate in activities. However, it is very difficult and time consuming for educators to thoroughly track and assess all the activities performed by all learners on all these tools. Moreover, it is hard to evaluate the structure of the course content and its effectiveness on the learning process. Resource providers do their best to structure the content assuming its efficacy. Educators, using Web-based learning environments, are in desperate need for non-intrusive and automatic ways to get objective feedback from learners in order to better follow the learning process and appraise the on-line course structure effectiveness. On the learner’s side, it would be very useful if the system could automatically guide the learner’s activities and intelligently recommend on-line activities or resources that would favour and improve the learning. These tools do not exist yet and to the best of our knowledge there is no distance leaning system to date that provides such automated facilities either on the learner’s side or educator’s side. In the field of electronic commerce, however, given the lucrative prospects, a significant research effort has been made to devise elaborate methods to take advantage of customers’ accesses and purchase behaviours in order to enhance the purchasing experience and customer satisfaction by user profiling and smart recommendations, and thus increase profit. For example, systems for recommendation such as Amazon.com that suggests books to purchase related to a current purchase based on preference information and similar user purchases, or recommendation of movies with moviefinder.com, use collaborative filtering which predicts a person’s preferences as a linear weighted combination of other people’s preferences. Recently, researchers have used web access history to make web sites more adaptive and personalized and hence more attractive to visitors, which is critical to keep customers loyal. WUM [8] is a special web sequence analyser for improving web pages layout and structure based on the history of access sequences. Entire conferences and workshops have been dedicated to web usage analysis for the benefit of e-commerce [10,11,12]. While the analogy with e-commerce seems straight forward, it is certainly not as simple as it appears. It is true that in e-commerce the goal is to increase sales and profit and it is achieved by understanding customer access behaviour [2], and in elearning the goal might be to improve the learning and it could be also achieved by understanding learners’ access patterns. However, many concepts involved are fundamentally different. For instance a purchase transaction, hence a session, which is a fundamental building block for most web usage mining algorithms, is somehow defined starting from a initial access to the web site to a purchasing or order operation, usually in a very short time frame (i.e. the same access session). In e-learning, a learning session can span many access sessions. To learn a concept or attain an exact result in a quiz, many access sessions, spread over many days and even weeks may be needed. Moreover, while the goal in e-commerce sites may be clear, for example encouraging the customers to buy more products and keeping them loyal, the goals in e-learning are vague, difficult to qualify/quantify and subjective. Web-based course delivery systems, like any web site or web-based application, rely on web servers to provide access to resources and applications. Every single request that a Web server receives is recorded in an access log mainly registering the origin of the request, a time stamp and the resource requested, whether the request is for a web page containing an article from a course chapter, the answer to an on-line exam question, or a participation in an on-line conference discussion. The web log provides a raw trace of the learners’ navigation and activities on the site. In order to process these log entries and extract valuable patterns that could be used to enhance the learning system or help in the learning evaluation, a significant cleaning and transformation phase needs to take place so as to prepare the information for data mining algorithms. The following section presents the issues related to web log cleaning and transformation. Section 3 enumerates some important data mining tasks that can be adopted in web usage mining. Section 4 illustrates with examples how web usage mining can be useful to enhance web-based learning environments. Finally, Section 5 presents some concluding remarks. 2. Web Log Cleansing There is an assortment of web log analysis tools available [2]. Most of them, like NetTracker, webtrends, analog and SurfAid, etc., provide limited statistical analysis of web log data [16]. For example, a typical report has entries of the form: "during this time period t, there were n clicks occurring for this particular web page p". However, the results provided by these tools are limited in their abilities to help understand the implicit usage information and hidden trends. New products use more sophisticated and complex analytic means but are generic, require important manual intervention and often resort to sampling due to the huge size of web logs [2]. The most commonly used method to evaluate access to web resources or user interest in resources is by counting page accesses or “hits”. However, this is not sufficient and often not correct. Web server log files of current common web servers contain insufficient data upon which to base thorough analysis. However, they contain useful data from which a well-designed data mining system can discover beneficial information. Web server log files customarily contain: the domain name (or IP address) of the request; the user name of the user who generated the request (if applicable); the date and time of the request; the method of the request (GET or POST); the name of the file requested; the result of the request (success, failure, error, etc.); the size of the data sent back; the URL of the referring page; the identification of the client agent; and a cookie, a sting of data generated by an application and exchanged between the client and the server. A log entry is automatically added each time a request for a resource reaches the web server. While this may reflect the actual use of the resources on a site, it does not record reader behaviours like frequent backtracking or frequent reloading of the same resource when the resource is cached by the browser or a proxy. It is important to note that the entries of all users are mixed in the log, simply ordered chronologically even though one single page request from a user may generate multiple entries in the server log. One major problem in web log mining is to identify unique users and associate users with their access log entries. In e-learning applications, however, the problem is simplified since users are not anonymous but need to login to the system as registered learners. However, identifying sessions is a non-trivial task. The goal is to identify sequences of activities from the collection of mixed log entries as described above, and model them as sessions of learning activities to be presented to the educators for evaluation and interpretation, or forwarded to advanced data mining tools to further discover intrinsic useful patterns. The major steps for web log data transformation can be summarized as follows: • • • • • • Remove irrelevant entries Identify access sessions Map access log entries to learning activities Complete traversal paths Group access sessions by learner to identify learning sessions Integrate with other data about learners and groups of learners Removing irrelevant entries is the simple task of weeding out requests for images, for example, or non-user requests such as web crawler requests etc. Identifying sessions is a ÎÎÎÎ demanding task. The aim is to recognize sequences of events such as A B C B D… where A, B, C, D, etc. are page or script requests. The challenge is to recognize the beginning and the end of sessions. The problem comes from the fact that HTTP, the protocol used for information exchange between web servers and browsers, is stateless and does not keep track of semantic sessions. In e-commerce applications, the end of sessions are usually the purchase of a product or the checkout of an e-cart, and idle times between requests that exceed 25 to 30 minutes are use to identify cuts between sessions. This heuristic is not necessarily true in the on-line learning context since learners can wander in other sites gathering relevant information while their access session at the e-learning site is still on hold. Moreover a learning session can span over days with different accesses. Many pages in elearning applications are dynamically generated by script requests such as quiz pages, conference messages, etc. Mapping access log entries with actual learning activities consists of replacing script calls with their assigned parameter values with concrete activities. This is an arduous task that assumes thorough knowledge of the application scripts and their respective parameters and requires a mapping table provided by the application designers. The result is a sequence of learners’ relevant on-line activities of the form: Login ÎExerciseListÎSubmissionQuiz1ÎExerciseListÎReadConferenceMessage… Completing the traversal paths consists of inferring cache hits and proxy meddling based on the structure of the web site and how pages and activities are effectively linked together. Finally, integrating the cleaned click streams with existing data about learners can be very valuable and beneficial. Such data could be the profiles of the learners, their quantitative and qualitative evaluations, etc. For instance combining the grades associated with completed activities with the sequences of events leading to these activities can help discover appropriate patterns that can help discriminate between sequence of activities that yield good results and sequence of events that are not as effective. The web log cleaning and transformation phase often consumes 80% to 95% of the effort and resources needed for web usage mining [2]. The result of the pre-processing is a database of sets of pertinent activity sequences grouped by learner. This is usually modeled with sequences of tokens associated with user identification stored in flat files that current data mining algorithms can act upon. The information can also be stored in a data warehouse like in [16] allowing ad-hoc online analytical processing. The other two phases after data preprocessing are pattern discovery using intricate data mining algorithms, and pattern evaluation [9]. 3. Useful Data Mining Tasks What is needed are summarization trends and patterns that can be interpreted by educators delivering their courses on-line. Due to the importance of e-commerce and the lucrative opportunities behind understanding on-line customer purchasing behaviours, there is tremendous research effort in developing data mining algorithms and systems tailored for e- business related web usage data mining [4]. In addition to descriptive statistical analysis provided by most web access log analysis tools such as calculating hit frequency, average, median, etc., length and duration of sessions and other limited low-level statistical measures, there have been some data mining approaches adapted specifically for web usage mining. The most used methods are association rules mining, clustering, classification, sequential pattern analysis and dependency modeling [9], as well as prediction. These techniques are primarily used for personalization, system improvement such as web caching and network traffic improvements, site modification, and marketing intelligence [9]. None of these applications, however, was tailored to distance learning, but the methods are general enough that e-learning systems could benefit from them. Association rules generation is the discovery of relationships between items in transactions. It is typically used for market basket analysis to discover rules of the form “x% of customers who buy item A and B also buy item C.” Clustering is an unsupervised grouping of objects, while classification is a supervised grouping. In web mining, the objects could be users, events, sessions, pages, etc. Sequential pattern analysis is similar to association rules but takes into account the sequences of events. In other words, the fact that a page A is requested before another page B is captured in the patterns discovered. All these techniques were designed for knowledge discovery from very large databases of numerical data [6] and were adapted for web mining and applied in on-line business with relative success. 4. Enhancing Web-Based Learning Environments WebSIFT [1] is a set of comprehensive web usage tools that is able to perform many data mining tasks and discover a variety of patterns from web logs. A versatile system, WebLogMiner [16], uses data warehousing technology for pattern discovery and trend summarization from web logs. However these wide-ranging tools are not integrated in elearning systems and it is cumbersome for an educator who doesn’t have extensive knowledge in data mining to use these tools to improve the effectiveness of web-based learning environments. A new web usage mining system dedicated for e-learning is being developed to allow educators to assess on-line learning activities [15]. For an educator using a web-based course delivery environment, it could be beneficial to track the activities happening in the course web site and extract patterns and behaviours prompting needs to change, improve, or adapt the course contents. For example, one could identify the paths frequently and regularly visited, the paths never visited, the clusters of learners based on the paths they follow, etc. For a learner using a web-based course delivery environment, it could be beneficial to receive hints from the system on what subsequent activity to perform based on similar behaviour by other “successful” learners. For example, the system could suggest shortcuts to frequently visited pages based on previous user activities, or suggest activities that made similar learners more “successful”. It could also be beneficial if the system adapts the course content logical structure to the learner’s learning pace, interest, or previous behaviour. Web-based course content is not always presented and structured in an intuitive way. By analyzing common traversal paths of the course content web pages or frequent changes in individual traversal paths, the layout of the course can be reorganized or adapted to better fit the needs of a group or an individual. We see two types of data mining in the context of e-learning: off-line web usage mining and integrated web usage mining. Off-line web usage mining is the discovery of patterns with a standalone application. This pattern discovery process would allow educators to assess the access behaviours, validate the learning models used, evaluate the learning activities, compare learners and their access patterns, etc. We have designed and implemented a prototype of such an application as a tool for educators to apply association rules to discover relationships between learning activities that learners perform, sequential analysis to discover interesting patterns in the sequences of on-line activities, and clustering to group similar access behaviours [15]. While most data mining algorithms need specific parameters and threshold values to tune the discovery process, the users of web usage mining applications in the context of e-learning, namely educators and e-learning site designers, are not necessarily savvy in the intricate complexities of data mining algorithms. For this purpose we have tried to design new algorithms that need minimum input from the user and automatically adjust to the web log data at hand. In [3] we propose a totally non-parametric approach for clustering web sessions. Off-line web usage mining helps educators put in question and validate the learning models they use as well as the structure of the web site as it is perused by the learners. In contrast, integrated web usage mining is a process of discovering patterns that is incorporated with the e-learning application. This encompasses adaptive web sites, personalization of activities, and automatic recommenders that suggest activities to learners based on their preferences as well as their history of activities and the access patterns discovered from the communal accesses. We are currently designing a recommender based association rule mining similar to the text categorization we developed in [14]. The idea consists of discovering relevant associations between learning activities and generating association rules that are applied in real time when in a current session the activities of the antecedent of a rule are verified then the activities in the consequent of the rule are suggested to the learner as the recommended next step in the learning session. The algorithm for text categorization presented in [14] can also be used to automatically categorize learners’ messages sent on an asynchronous conferencing system in order to help the educators better assess the information exchange in a course related forum. 5. Conclusions and Future Work The Web is an excellent tool to deliver on-line courses in the context of distance education. However, counting only on web traffic statistical analysis does not take advantage in the potential of hidden patterns inside the web logs. Web usage mining is a non-trivial process of extracting useful implicit and previously unknown patterns from the usage of the Web. Significant research is invested to discover these useful patterns to increase profitability of ecommerce sites. However, the goals of these applications and methods, “turning visitors into purchasers”, are different from the goals in e-learning: “turning learners into effective better learners.” We have seen some examples where data mining techniques can enhance on-line education for the educators as well as the learners. While some tools using data mining techniques to help educators and learners are being developed, the research is still in its infancy. In addition, with the awareness of the potential advantages of integrated web usage mining and the insufficient data recorded by web servers, there is a need for more specialized logs from the application side to enrich the information already logged by the web server. This added value by specific event recording on the elearning side will give clicksteams and the patterns discovered a better meaning and interpretation. References [1] R. Cooley, B. Mobasher, J.
